speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are three motions standing on the Order Paper at the report stage of Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act. Motions Nos. 1 and 2, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), should be grouped for debate but voted separately. Motion No. 3, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), will be debated and voted on separately.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Deans (for Mr. Orlikow) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, be amended in Clause 3 by striking out line 20 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"obligation for the acquisition of depreciable assets, or the financing of
research and development, or to meet operating expenses and owed by him, the
Minister may,".
Motion No. 2.
That Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, be amended in Clause 3 by striking out line 5 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"the grant is made to not less than ten per".

Mr. Speaker, we have had the opportunity of discussing this Bill and the implications associated with it, as articulated by the Members of the New Democratic Party in particular. I want to take a moment or two to refer to the specific nature of these amendments and the reasons for them.
When one looks at the content of Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act, one's first reaction is to be supportive, to recognize it as a positive step in the right direction. It is the Government once again recognizing its obligation to assist the small business sector. If there is a sector of our country that has been overlooked by the federal Government, it is the small business sector. If one were to examine all of the various programs that have been implemented over the years to provide some assistance for the business community, and I use the business community in the broadest sense as
including the agricultural sector, the fishing sector and the like, one would find that very few programs have been introduced to provide assistance to the small business sector specifically.
Large businesses-the corporate sector, the international business community-have a variety of programs designed to assist and encourage them, but by and large the small business sector has been overlooked, particularly when it comes to assistance that is real to them. Once again, I am afraid, Bill C-136 has missed the mark. It is a Bill that says to the small business sector that if they are interested in expanding their operation, particularly in terms of new equipment, we are prepared to assist them at this time.
[DOT] (mo)
Mr. Speaker, I do not expect that there is a single Member sitting in the House of Commons today who feels that the problem the small business sector is facing today is one of adding new equipment to their operation. The problem of the small business sector today is simply one of survival. Small business people across this country at this moment are clinging on by their Fingertips on a daily basis waiting for the banks to move in, waiting for the financial companies that they depend on to foreclose.
It is now the spring season when the small business sector traditionally begins to grow and expand its operation and new jobs are created. But I am afraid that is not occurring in the spring of 1983. If you were to sit down and analyze what was happening to the small business sector in every region of this country, the small business sector is disappearing from the Canadian landscape and being replaced by the international chains, by the corporate sector.
Now, one could simply debate in itself whether or not it is to Canada's advantage to have the corporate sector predominating and growing at the expense of the small business community. I do not think there is any question in terms of the longterm viability of our Canadian economy that we have to be paying more attention to the small, family-oriented business, the business that has a commitment to its community, the business that is 100 per cent Canadian owned and Canadian controlled, the business that has a commitment to Canada, to its Province, to its sub-region and to its community. The international corporation does not have that. Its priority is to its shareholders and more often than not to foreign shareholders and to a foreign board of directors. What we are talking about in this particular Bill, a Bill called the Small Business Investment Grants Act, is a minute step in the right direction

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
and these amendments address two of the significant weaknesses in this Bill.
Let me take a moment or two to talk about those two weaknesses. The problem is that small businesses today have difficulty obtaining funds for expansion, for buying new equipment and new plants. Small businesses today are having problems operating and just simply staying in business. Most small businesses have cut back on their employees, have cut out all of their expansion plans, have closed off whatever sectors they are able to close off, and are left with the bare bones of their small business operation.

Amendment No. 1 says that the Government has an obligation to assist the small business community during these very difficult times in two critical areas. The first critical area and the most important is assistance with working capital. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) is knowledgeable about the plight of the small business community and knows full well that it is lack of working capital that is causing difficulty out there today. I am sure that if he had his way he would support amendment No. 1, so I hope he does get his way. I suspect that it is his Cabinet colleagues who are holding back.
This would cost the Government some money but there is no alternative. If this sector of our economy disappears from the landscape it will mean a further erosion of the economy, fewer revenues flowing into Government coffers and more flowing out in terms of social assistance programs. We must reverse this tide and the way to do that is to provide assistance to those businesses that are having problems with working capital and through the provision of research and development money.
The small business sector of our economy is going to perform the major part in a recovery program for Canada. That is because it is able to move quickly and take advantage of the changing times much more than the cumbersome international corporation can with its inertia of bureaucracy. The small business community is able to dodge and weave, move and twist and turn to take advantage of the changes in our society. We should encourage that, Mr. Speaker. We should encourage the small business community to come up with ideas for research, for opening up new product lines, for new marketing strategies. We should be behind it 100 per cent, but we are not, Mr. Speaker. If we could assist the community with this particular borrowing procedure then we should do so.
We are not doing that, Mr. Speaker, and that is why the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and myself have decided to offer an amendment that would provide encouragement to the small business sector to carry out aggressive policies, from research and development through to production, and to provide assistance to businesses hard pressed for operating capital. It is a step in the right direction, Mr. Speaker.
I should like now to refer to the second amendment, Mr. Speaker. We feel that there is a psychological barrier that must be broken in this country if we are to give a very clear signal to the small business community that we are on side and
expect it to lead a major effort in this recovery. That signal is the level of interest that a small business person must pay when he or she approaches the bank for operating funds or for new development lines.
At the moment, the Bill allows that the interest rate could drop to 12 per cent. That is not particularly comforting, Mr. Speaker. As a matter of fact, it is a jolt. The small business community, 900,000 strong, is waiting for an indication of how seriously the Government considers its plight, and the Government is introducing a Bill to allow it to borrow money at 12 per cent for new plant. That is not a revolutionary breakthrough in terms of assistance to the small business community. If someone went to the FBDB or the Royal Bank of Canada or any lending institution now, they could probably get that same rate.
We should give this Bill some guts, Mr. Speaker, and introduce measures that will assist the small business community. One way to do that, as the amendment suggests, is to provide that the rate be 10 per cent. To my mind that is a psychological point. If we can provide money to the small business community at 10 per cent, it will give encouragement to expand; but during these times, 12 per cent offers little incentive.
With those two amendments, Mr. Speaker, we urge the Official Opposition to support us, but, more important, we urge Members of the Government to give a clear signal to the small business community by supporting amendments Nos. 1 and 2. I know the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism would accept them if he has the support of his caucus colleagues.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make some comments on the amendments proposed by my colleague. I have a great deal of respect for his knowledge of the small business community and the concern that he has expressed not only today but in the weeks and months gone by. He knows, and I know, that we are dealing today with a Bill which was introduced on October 28 and which has had, in my opinion, and I suspect in his opinion also, a far too lengthy passage through this House. In fact, what we are dealing with is an instrument which was brought in at a time when interest rates were high, and we are dealing with it now at report stage and third reading at a time when interest rates have come down substantially from where they were when the instrument was first introduced.
I believe we must ask ourselves, is this the instrument for the future? Do we want a better instrument than this to serve the small business community? I agree with the Hon. Member that a signal must be sent to the small business community. I want to send it and I believe the Hon. Member wants to send it also. Let us send the message today to the small business community that we realize that they are the main piston in the
April 11, 1983

engine of the economy, which is private enterprise. They are the job creators. Forty-two per cent of all the jobs in Canada are held in small business. If we want to create jobs we must support them. I realize the business community wants working capital. I know they want to plan expansion now. But is this the best instrument now?
I have been speaking with my small business consultative committee from across the country and we have been consulting with other groups which represent the small business community. We hope very soon to put out a small business strategy, which would be the strategy of the Government of Canada for the support of small business. The question is, however, is a Bill which was introduced on October 28, and which is now receiving final disposition today, the best instrument to support small business for the future? I would urge the Hon. Member and the Official Opposition to pass this Bill today because, really, what we are talking about is an instrument which has served over the years. Indeed, the program went into effect without the legislation. The brochures went out very quickly. We were able to use a vote within Industry, Trade and Commerce to support some of the applications, except for those from farmers and fishermen which, by the way, totalled 62 per cent of the applications under the SBIG. Sixty-two per cent of the applications were from farmers and fishermen from all across the country.
I ask for quick disposition of this Bill because it is a measure which expired, according to the period announced in the budget, on March 31. The information was put in the brochures and on the application forms. Everyone was aware publicly that this was a temporary measure while interest rates were high and which was to expire on March 31.1 say to the Opposition now that we should deal with this because 62 per cent of those who applied will not be able to receive the money which we have committed to them. I do not know how many farmers and fishermen there are in Mississauga, but there are many across the country who will not be able to take advantage of this measure. There are 4,000 applications made under this program to date. I am urging the Opposition to accept speedy passage of this Bill so that we can keep our commitment to the farmers and fishermen and the other people who have applied under this program. As I say, it was a measure which was introduced when interest rates were high and I believe what we have to look at now is a much more comprehensive strategy for the support of small business.
While I appreciate the point raised by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), that working capital has to be supplied, I would remind him, and I know he knows full well, there are instruments such as the Federal Business Development Bank and such as EDP, which indeed do provide for loans for working capital. What I believe we should be focusing on is our normal lending institutions, our normal lending mechanisms and vehicles. This is a temporary measure and we should be looking now to refine our normal lending mechanisms to support small business. 1 appreciate the fact that he says that interest rates are still high, as indeed they are, for
Small Business Investment Grants Act
small business, but they are coming down. I believe we should let market forces continue to work so that they will, as I believe they will, come down in favour of small business.
I appreciate the points made by the Hon. Member, but I say to him let us pass this legislation without amendment now because it is a temporary measure which we have used, and let us look to the future for our policy towards small business. Let us refine our existing lending mechanism so that we can give a clear signal to small business that it has to be the focus, as we come out of this recession. We are for them and we are going to put in place those instruments that they need; but this is not necessarily the best vehicle.

Mr. Speaker, can the Minister advise us where in the Bill this measure is limited to March 31, 1983. I notice in his blue and green publicity document that it was limited to March 31, but where in the Bill is there any limit on the life of this grant program?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, number one, it was in the budget.
Which budget?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: This is a budget measure, Mr. Speaker. It was limited quite specifically in the budget to March 31. So first of all it is a budgetary item; it was also put in the regulations which we had hoped would be passed long before now, of course, and in all the literature which has been made public in connection with this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, if it was in the budget, maybe the Minister could tell us where. I have the budget speech here and I do not see where there is a limitation on this program of March 31, 1983. Was it the intention of the Government definitely to limit the program to that date? If that is the case, will the Minister be seeking unanimous consent of the House to amend the Bill so that it will provide only retroactive approval of advances made under this Bill up to and including March 31, 1983?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have to repeat the point I made. We are talking about a measure which was developed when interest rates were high. We are talking about commitments which had been made and a program which would finish March 31, with other mechanisms to follow in its place. I urge the Opposition to pass this measure as quickly as possible so that indeed we can keep our commitments. I think speedy passage would be in the interest of those people who have been seeking help and support under this program up until now.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister's answers point out the very reason why the House should defeat this Bill. I say that because the Government has no intention at this point of using this measure as a grant program to assist small business to reduce interest costs. Indeed, the Government dillied around with Bill C-136,

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
refusing to bring it on for debate when there was a need for assistance on interest rates. Interest rates have now fallen to the point where the prime rate is 11.5 per cent, so a Bill which subsidizes interest rates to 12 per cent is not much of an assistance program. The fact is that the Government has all of the mileage it wants out of this Bill.
I want to remind the House that the then Minister of Finance, in order to curry the favour of small business, on June 28 last said:
I am announcing an important new program to reduce interest costs for small businesses undertaking new investment. $400 million is being allocated to this program.
The expansion of many small businesses has been halted by high interest rates. Grants will therefore be made to cover four percentage points of interest charges, over a period of two years, on loans extended by financial institutions to both incorporated and unincorporated small businesses.
There was nothing mentioned about limitation of the grants or anything of that nature. The budget was immediately produced and another fancy brochure was produced describing what this Government would do for small business. The small business community knows what the Government has done to small business. It has raped and pillaged small business. It has taxed and regulated it to death and has destroyed it.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I understand that unanimous consent was given to the Hon. Member to ask questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has been recognized to make a speech.

The former Minister continues to rise occasionally in the House without understanding for what purpose he is doing so.
The fact is that the Government's programs for small business have remained largely at the brochure stage. We have seen such brochures as "ABCs for Small Business" and the "Government of Canada in the Small Business Community". Other brochures have been published by DREE along with other documents from various other sources.
In order to understand what the small business community wants, I would like to refer the House to the evidence given by John Bulloch, President of the Federation of Independent Business, to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on September 16, 1982. At that time he said:
You can get rid of half the grant and aid programs for small business in Canada. They were all created by bureaucrats in response to Ministers' questions. What can I do for small business, they are putting the heat on me? And up comes another program.
There has been no program in this country developed or asked for by us at the provincial level, and there are something like 800 of them. You could scrap half of them. Go back to the tax system, and you can get a lot of financing. If you want to start cutting budgets and cut into the business sector, we will give you all the support. We say you should be making absolute cuts in the cost of Government and cut into the business sector as well as all your other areas. They do not reach the people you want to reach. They are the bureaucratic response to political pressures. They are bubbling up all over the place; they never stop. And we have never asked for anything.
This was said by the President of the Federation of Independent Business and this program represents exactly that. Our colleagues in the New Democratic Party have put forward an amendment which essentially says that if the Government really means it all, then why not make these grants to subsidsize interest to not less than 10 per cent? Those modest Members in the NDP suggest only 10 per cent.
A review of the interest rates in this country shows that while the Bank of Canada rate is 9.5 per cent, the Government has permitted the chartered banks to set their prime rate at 2 per cent above the Bank of Canada rate. That differential is unheard of since the differential between the prime rate and the Bank of Canada rate used to be somewhere between one-half per cent and three-quarters per cent. The Government has permitted that differential to rise to 2 per cent and remain that way for a number of months.
The Government has the authority and responsibility to drive this country's prime rate down and direct the banks to do so. The fact is that the bank prime rates are significantly higher than they should be. There is no justification for a Government that really pretended to want to help small business to produce this Bill and ask for its speedy passage, knowing that it will do nothing for anyone. The Government refers to farmers and fishermen but it does not give us any statistics on the amount of money involved and why they were included in the Bill initially instead of being covered under other appropriate legislation dealing with farmers and fishermen.
The Government has indicated that it will not accept a proposal that would reduce interest rates for small business to 10 per cent. It is inconceivable that this Government of propaganda and puffery should be allowed to get away with it. I hope that the debate today, tomorrow and perhaps another day will allow us to point out the fraudulent and deceitful nature of the presentations we have heard from the Government with respect to small business. The amendments to the Bill call the Government to task. The amendments suggest that if the Government plans to take action, it should do something about inventory and the cost of working capital. It should strive to drive interest rates down to a level where business can begin to make a profit.
The Government does not do this because it would have to pay something for its advertising program. I suspect that the Government has spent about as much money for puffing up this program in its cross-country advertising as it will spend on grants under the program itself. There is nothing like $400 million in grants. We have not heard the Minister or the Government tell us how much money it has committed to this program. However, the committee received some figures back in December, and since they were modest at that time I suspect they will become even more modest as interest rates drop. If Members seriously analyze the advertising and puffery associated with the program, I suspect they would find almost as much money is spent on advertising and puffery as is spent on grants.
April 11, 1983

Therefore, we are faced with a situation in which we have a Minister who purports to act on behalf of small business. He purports to be the Minister for small business and he comes to the House to ask us to pass his Bill. He does this so he may put another notch in his rifle to show what he has done for the business community. He is a Minister who does not really have any clout, power, desire or energy to act on behalf of small business. He merely enjoys issuing his brochures but does not accomplish anything. If these amendments are not passed, it is proof positive that he will not do anything.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in regard to this matter. The Hon. Minister pointed out that the Bill was introduced on October 28, 1982. It is amazing that the Minister advises us today that the Bill expired on March 31, 1983. That was 11 days ago. In other words, we are being asked to pass a Bill which has already expired. Therefore, those people who were waiting for the Bill to pass so that they could apply for grants will now be unable to apply unless the Minister assures us that applications will be accepted under this Bill for a period of three months or six months from the time it has passed. Otherwise, it is utterly unfair. The normal procedure is for people to wait for a Bill to be passed before they make application. Those who would benefit but have not made application to date are completely out of luck unless the Minister makes that change. I think that assurance has to come. Otherwise we are almost wasting our time.
If it is possible, I would like the minister to tell us how many applications have been received to date. It would be interesting to see how many people really believed the legislation would be passed and applied under the Bill. I submit again that it is utterly unfair to bar people from applying for this benefit because the Bill was not passed before March 31. I urge the Minister at least to make this reasonably fair so that people can apply after the Bill is passed. This only makes ordinary, everyday sense.
The Bill is limited. I like the two amendments introduced by our friends in the New Democratic Party. They certainly improve the Bill and they are being debated together. The real problem today is still high interest rates. The 4 per cent remains in the Bill. There is a maximum of 12 per cent, unless the amendment down to 10 per cent is accepted. This means that a person with an 18 per cent interest rate would obtain a benefit of 4 per cent but would still be paying 14 per cent. Someone with an interest rate of 20 per cent-and there are a number of people over that-would obtain 16 per cent. Those with 14 per cent interest rates under the Bill would only obtain a 2 per cent advantage. If the amendments carry, at least these would obtain a 4 per cent advantage.
I realize that it was not this Minister who introduced the Bill, but he is now carrying responsibility for it. I ask him who we are trying to help?
I have just spent a number of days mainstreeting in my constituency. The real problem faced by farms and small
Small Business Investment Grants Act
businesses-and farms are small businesses as well-is that people are locked into interest rates. They had to renew at 17, 18, 19 or 20 per cent rates; they had no choice. Back in November the present Minister spoke on second reading and mentioned that $400 million was being provided to help with up to 4 per cent of interest, and this is what the Bill indicates, $400 million.
Recently the agricultural Members of the Progressive Conservative Party submitted a proposal to the Government that would cost $100 million, by which we could buy out all those high interest rates from our farmers. We could buy out those 16 per cent to 22 per cent interest rates for less than $100 million and then have the loans refinanced so that they will pay a stable interest rate. If we do something like that, we would be doing something for small business.
This Bill will be a drop in the bucket. It is too little, it is too late; it is only a drop in the bucket. It does not tackle the real problem bothering small businesses today.
I urge the Hon. Minister to bring in amendments. He could do so with the consent of the House. He could bring in amendments that would take $100 million of that $400 million and really do a job by buying out the highest interest rates, because these people really had no choice.
I do not know how many applications have been received, but the normal procedure is that people do not apply until the Bill is passed. We will not help those who have gone into receivership or gone bankrupt. It is too late for them, but we may still help many people to stay on the land and to stay in business.
Surely, if this Bill has any objective at all, it should be to keep our businessmen, farmers, fishermen and all small-businessmen viable. It is small business upon which we depend for jobs. It is small-business people who went out of business. Sure, we lost many jobs through the big boys, those firms which employed from 2,000 to 4,000 people, but many of the two million are unemployed now as a result of small businesses going bankrupt, laying off help, bringing in their wives to help because they could not afford to pay anyone from the outside, and having their children of all ages help in the store and on the farm. That is how some of them remained viable. Some farmers have gone out and worked at other jobs just to keep their farms going.
This Bill will be of help to some, but not to very many if we do not extend the application date. It could be a great deal of help if the Minister would really do a job of buying out the high interest rates and refinancing at a reasonable level.
There are other things which should be done. As the Minister mentioned, the Bill will not solve all problems. It is too bad it was not passed back in November. I really do not know why it was not. I think there would have been unanimous consent on all sides of the House for this Bill to come in. I do not know why it has taken five months, from November to March, when we took time in the House to deal with Bills which the people do not want, such as Canagrex. We wasted two full days. One

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
of those days could have been used to pass this Bill. To rush it now, I think we have to have assurance from the Minister that people will still be able to make application, those it will help. Let us help as many as we can. The more we can help, the better. If the change I just mentioned is made, it could help a lot more people.
There are many things which should and could be done to help keep small businesses, farms and our fishing sector viable. It would not cost the Government one cent to keep many farms viable. It could simply change a small section of the Western Grain Stabilization Act, where it would make a pay-out in three years instead of five years. It would put perhaps $150 million into the pockets of farmers who are part of the program involving wheat, oats and barley. It would keep them viable.
I know a farmer who on paper today is rich. He is a relatively young man. He went to college. He obtained his Bachelor of Science degree in agriculture. Now he is rich on paper but almost bankrupt because there is no cash flow. This Bill will not help him very much. These people need help.
I see my speaking time has come to an end. Before sitting down I urge the Minister to bring in some measure with real meat in it to help small-businessmen, farmers and fishermen. They need it, as the Hon. Minister knows.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we are here today to begin debate at report stage on a Bill, as was mentioned earlier by previous speakers, that was introduced for first reading almost six months ago, Bill C-136 respecting the Small Business Investment Grants Act. It formally enacts certain measures that arose out of one of the series of budgets brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) or his predecessor to try and repair some of the damage caused by earlier budgets. To some extent it marks a departure for the Government for, like most of its predecessors, it does little good and, unlike most of them, it does little harm either. Perhaps that is a step in the right direction for this Government and one for which we should congratulate them.
As a Bill, what does it purport to achieve? Not very much that I can see. Essentially it empowers the Minister to make regulations, and that is about all it does. At the present time, it is a near totally irrelevant Bill. At a time when interest rates and the measures contained in the Government's many budgets combine to squeeze the life out of small businesses' working capital, it expressly excludes loans for the purpose of providing working capital.
As my colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) mentioned, he was on the hustings during the Easter recess. I too talked to many businessmen in my riding who pointed out the crying need for working capital, asking where they could get money to stay afloat, they are that close to the line. It is no good
providing money to firms already in receivership or bankruptcy.
At a time when the Government's measures have made the purchase of new equipment out of the question for most small businesses, it expressly excludes loans for the purpose of buying used equipment. In short, it displays all the foresight and the understanding of the plight of small business that we have come to expect of this Government.
But wait. It goes even further in displaying the Government's firm grasp of the realities of life in the private sector. We on this side of the aisle have for many, many years been harping on the need for providing incentives whereby industry may step up its research and development. Lo and behold, we find that expenditures for research and development, if engaged in by small business and funded by borrowing, are eligible for inclusion in this program.
I do not want to take anything away from those small firms which have been forced to borrow to finance their research and development, but surely wherever possible a company tries to meet these costs out of earnings. Of course, it depends on the definition one applies to research and development, but for the most part it is just not the sort of thing that a company borrows to pay for.
In other words, the inclusion of research and development under the terms of this Act is not the sort of move that is calculated to strengthen and support Canadian research. Rather, it gives the impression that it is an item thrown in at the last minute so as to be pointed at later as evidence of the Government's deep and abiding concern for research and development in Canada. In short, it follows along in the new familiar Liberal tradition of not doing much good, but at least being something to crow about later. I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will excuse the pun in introducing the word "crow".
Surely the country has a right to expect better of its Government at a time like this. What else is new? The Government is tired. It is spiritually worn out and mentally exhausted. This is the best, literally, that it can come up with. How much better it would be for the entire nation if it were to shuffle quietly off to wherever mortally ill Governments, like elephants, go to die.
The classic irony of it all is, of course, that this Bill offers grants to cover interest charges on small business loans down to a limit of 12 per cent. It is all good stuff, except that the current prime rate is only 11.5 per cent. Inasmuch as small business loan rates are one to two points over prime, once again we see the Government just a little out of step with reality.
As mentioned previously, there is no question that businessmen on their own can in all probability negotiate loans without the assistance provided in this Bill. However, that really is of limited importance at the present time because the Bill has already been in effect for at least six months. I suppose that is what upsets me most about this Bill; it is not what it does, which within its limitations is good, even if it could have been done so much better. So, the most upsetting thing is the way in which it has been introduced.
April 11, 1983

After the measures legalized in this Bill have been in effect for almost six months, we are asked to debate the legislation at report stage. To do so is a waste of time. There are many more important matters that we should be addressing. Most significantly, that it should be introduced in this fashion speaks volumes about the esteem in which this House is held by the Government.
This is the Government and the Party headed by the man who once declared that Members of Parliament were nobodies once they were 50 yards from Parliament Hill. How much more graphically can this opinion be underlined than by enforcing their writ throughout the country without bothering to legalize their actions for almost a year? Their actions tell us much about this Government. They tell us that they are disorganized almost to the point of confusion. Otherwise it would have produced a Bill better calculated to solve the problems it tries to deal with.
The Government tells us that it has an ill-concealed contempt for Parliament, the parliamentary process and ultimately for the Canadian public that this Parliament is elected to represent. Otherwise this Bill would have been dealt with expeditiously with the other budgetary measures when they were still fresh and meaningful. Lastly, it says a good deal about the Government's sense of values and priorities that it did not deal with these budgetary measures earlier, preferring first, for example, to get all the old age pensioners and Family Allowance recipients under the six and five program.
So be it. The Government has shown us its soul by its handling of these matters. It is a fait accompli; let us get it over with. However, we and the Canadian people will remember this Government's stewardship, sense of priorities and confusion. It has taken us for granted for too long. If the polls have anything at all to tell us, it is that the voters know this and are waiting.
I am well aware of the Minister's sympathy for small business. As he mentioned, there are a great many small businessmen, farmers and fishermen in his area. He stated that many applications have been submitted. I believe he mentioned 62 per cent, give or take 4,000. I wonder when they are going to be processed. Are not some being processed at the present time even though the Bill has not received third reading? The Minister can hardly say no one is able to take advantage of the Bill without it being passed.
There are many small businesses in my area of Parry Sound-Muskoka crying out for assistance to help keep them afloat and possibly to expand a bit. Needless to say, they want to do this with a more preferred interest rate than is available today. Thank goodness the rates are down considerably from a year ago.

Mr. Speaker, today I have ten minutes to speak about another example of the Liberal shell game. The Minister responsible for small businesses stood in this House and said that the Bill was introduced at the end of October and, therefore, it is time to get it through the House and passed. He also indicated that the Bill is the result of a budget introduced well over a year ago. The
Small Business Investment Grants Act
last time I looked at the regulations for Parliament, it was the job of the Government to propose legislation and the job of the Opposition and Members of Parliament to dispose of it.
We heard earlier today from the Minister responsible for small businesses a public admission of this government's failure to act. It is true that we had a budget over a year ago, it is true that interest rates were very high and that small business was hurting because of those interest rates.
A Government interested in action would have brought forward a piece of legislation of this kind immediately and given it a high priority on the parliamentary agenda. It would have passed and it might have done the country some good. However, for the Minister to stand in this House a year later and indicate there is some urgency for its passage when interest rates are down to the level of 12 per cent, which is specified in the Bill, is to admit that the Government of Canada failed to act when action was necessary.
To stand in the House and castigate the Opposition for not acting when action is no longer necessary is the height of hypocrisy. What has the Government done for small business? All it has done is to advertise a set of what looks like positive public intentions. It said to the small business community over a year ago, "You are in trouble when you are borrowing money; interest rates are too high, so we are going to do something about it and aren't we nice guys." Then it did nothing about it.
In that same budget, however, the Government did a lot of damage to small business. It was as if it said: "Over here on the left-hand side is the help. We will advertise the help which we are not delivering. We will say that we care when we really do not." But hidden in the budget and not advertised were measures like the half-year convention which reduced capital cost allowance to 50 per cent of its former level and hurt every small business in this country.
In that same budget, the Small Business Development Bond was turned into a bail-out bond. The Government turned it into a Catch-22 bond where only businesses that were facing bankruptcy would be eligible for Government assistance. They could go to the bank and attempt to borrow money, but those loans were not to be guaranteed by the Government. The bank had to take the risk and, of course, very few loans were granted. There is another source of help that disappeared. The survival bond did not work and the development bond was taken away from small business.
Deferred profit-sharing helped small business people and their employees prepare for retirement and at the same time put increased cash flow into those small businesses. In that same budget the Government took that away. It increased taxes on employee benefits. In other words, in that budget it took immediate action on a number of measures which hurt small business in this country, which made their survival less likely and their profitability almost impossible. As the Government did that, it did not have the courage to advertise those

things; it simply advertised that it was going to help those small businesses. First of all, it forced them to borrow more money and then it would help them with the borrowing cost.
The fact that we are standing in this Chamber today looking at the piece of legislation that was supposed to help a year ago tells us that the Government did not help. It hurt, but it did not help. What is particularly galling, and so common in legislation proposed by the Liberals since my time in this House, is that we get a piece of legislation and we are asked as Parliamentarians to try and amend it perhaps, but ultimately to vote for or against it. It involves the spending of taxpayers' money generally for some presumed positive social purpose. In most pieces of legislation, and certainly in this piece of legislation, you cannot find a single word about what such money is to be used for. What you find is a clause that says the Governor in Council shall make regulations. What that means is that the Cabinet shall decide who, if anybody, gets the money.
Are Cabinet decisions made in public? No. Are Parliamentarians invited to come before Cabinet and suggest what might work for the people in their riding or the people in this country? The answer to that is no. Cabinet decides on regulations in secret. Cabinet decides basically on recommendations that are put forward by civil servants, people who get a salary, who work for the Government, who do not face the threat of layoff, who do not have to meet productivity standards. They advise the Cabinet on what the regulations should be for small business. Where is the democracy in that? Where is the expert knowledge which small-businessmen represent? Who can speak to Cabinet on behalf of the small-businessmen of this nation?
If you look at some of the material which the Government has put out on this particular piece of legislation and its presumed help, you immediately spot the very first example of the lack of understanding that Cabinet and the civil service has of the world of the small-businessman. One of the small parts of this piece of legislation and the regulations which Cabinet is proposing for its implementation is to tell Canadian small-businessmen that if they buy a new piece of equipment, they are eligible for Government help. However, if they buy a used piece of equipment, they are not.
As a small-businessman who belongs to small business organizations and has done so for years, one who meets with small-business people on a regular basis, let me tell you that they are cost-conscious. One of the characteristics of the small-business people of this nation is that they do not have large amounts of money. Quite often their enterprises are sort of "Ma and Pa" operations, family operations with two, three or four employees. When true small businesses in this country of that size need a truck to deliver things in the city, they do not go out and buy a new truck; they go out and buy a used truck. That is the nature of small business. It is important that as the regulations for assistance in an Act of this kind come forward, those in this Chamber, Parliamentarians who are in touch with small business, have a say in where that money should go. It is
not right, it is not appropriate, and it is not helpful for Cabinet alone to make those decisions.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to discuss Bill C-136 which will provide the legislation necessary to implement the Small Business Investment Grants Program, the SBIG, as outlined in the June, 1982 budget. This program will provide grants of up to 4 per cent to reduce interest costs to as low as 12 percent for small businesses in Canada.
Before discussing the substance of C-136, I would like to examine the current state of small business in Canada to provide some insight into the necesssity and feasibility of the proposed legislation. Based on the findings released by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, to date in Canada there are between 700,000 and 800,000 fewer Canadians employed in the small and medium-sized business sector than there were in 1981. Small business has been hard-hit by the economic situation in Canada, which has worsened over the past couple of years. Over 50 per cent of the small businesses in the Canadian Federation of Independent Business have reported cutbacks in employee numbers during the past two years. These people have joined the ranks of the other
1,598,000	Canadians reported out of work as of January, 1983, not to mention the 500,000 Canadians no longer looking for work.
The President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has currently been urging the Government to adopt policies to bring down interest rates and encourage new business to be formed and existing businesses to expand. The development of small business is crucial to the country's economy and the sector's health is fundamental to any economic recovery.
Few businesses at the present time are making any plans for increasing their hiring or their investment. On a national basis 66.7 per cent expect to remain at the present employment level, 7.9 per cent reported they would hire additional people this year and another 9.1 per cent said they would rehire workers they were forced to lay off previously, while 8.2 per cent plan to employ fewer workers this year. Fully 82.3 per cent of the respondents to the CFIB survey have taken some measures of restraint, as 51 per cent reduced the number of employees and just under 30 per cent had present employees working reduced numbers of hours per week.
It is very clear to anyone, then, that the economic situation imposed on this country by our present Government has chronically damaged many small businesses in Canada and discouraged many businessmen from developing their own small businesses. The restraint placed on the small business owners and their employees has increased the already high unemployment rate and added to the dismal state of the economy.
Restraint measures, employment cutbacks and reduction of employee hours have occurred in all regions of Canada in
April 11, 1983

varying degrees. Restraint measures are at a high in British Columbia where firms imposing restraint have reached a level of 88.6 per cent, followed by Newfoundland at 87.1 per cent. In my own Province of Prince Edward Island, the reduction in employees is at a national high of 64 per cent, with the national average being 50.9 per cent, and it ranks third in the area of employee wage restraint in the independent business sector. How can any businessman be expected to have any confidence in the Canadian economy and general economic policies.
The small business community in Canada, with its entrepreneurial and innovative capabilities which can give us new products, processes, jobs and enterprise, is being dealt a heavy blow by our current economic situation and the present Government's economic policies. The desperately awaited business recovery will not occur without concrete and substantial changes in the business environment.
In view of these worries about public policy and the risk of interest rate increases, the responding businesses are making few plans as of now for increasing their hiring or investment. The independent business universe is a quilt of many patterns and colours. It includes many new firms just starting and growing, mature firms which are growing, and businesses which are being drastically changed to meet altered product demands or technological conditions, as well as many stable and mature firms. Interest rates remain a real concern for the small-businessman and they must be assured the rates will stay down before doing any hiring or investing.
The major factors identified as necessary to hire more workers are increased confidence in government policy and consistency and assurance that interest rates will not shoot up again. Businessmen are waiting for concrete and substantial evidence of a real change in governmental direction before committing themselves. They cannot be blamed for that. The small-businessman must ask the federal Government for concrete policies which will ensure him a stable economic recovery.
The hesitation of independent businesses to expand their operations is understandable when we examine the background of cutbacks they have been made to deal with due to our recession-a recession deliberately brought about by the federal Government. Small businesses have been affected by the restraint measures through the reduction in the number of their employees and the reduction of the employees' working hours per week. They have been forced to reduce or postpone wage increases for their employees and have been restricted in growth.
Wage restraints are even more hard hitting for small-businessmen than for their employees. Owners and managers have been forced to take reductions or lower increases in compensation. The largest element of restraint in a small business is in the area of employment. A good percentage of businesses have been forced to reduce the number of employees and, according to a questionnaire issued in January, 1981 and February, 1983, the net change for the respondents was 42,479 fewer employees.
Small Business Investment Grants Act
Traditionally the public sector has enjoyed effective job tenure. Recently, however, there have been notices of hiring freezes and even a few layoffs for public sector employees. From the results of a recent informal survey, it would appear that one to two thousand Government workers have been laid off and some 6,000 to 10,000 in CN, telephone companies, hospitals etc. This does not include several thousand casual workers which Governments have not kept on, and doubtless others in the numberless Crown corporations.
A further measure of restraint is the reduction in weekly hours of work for remaining employees. It is striking that just under 30 per cent of all respondents had reduced working hours per week. Laying off workers is a last resort for most firms, both because of concern for workers and because of the cost of recruiting and retraining workers later.
The impact of recession and restraint measures on the small business sector was relatively uniform across the country, yet to the extent that there were variations, the heaviest impact came at each end of the country. The response from British Columbia, Alberta, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland indicates that about 88 per cent of businesses had imposed restraint measures. Saskatchewan and New Brunswick were at the low end with 76 per cent each. British Columbia and Alberta had experienced more rapid economic growth for several years up to 1982, and had experienced a more rapid relative decline. This was shown in earlier surveys in 1981 and 1982 conducted by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
The same regional and provincial differences show up in reduced numbers of employees. In British Columbia and Alberta, 63 per cent and 59 per cent respectively of respondents indicated they had reduced the number of employees, compared to 51 per cent nationally. For Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland the percentages were 64 and 58 respectively. On the other hand, in Saskatchewan only 41 per cent of firms indicated they had laid workers off.
The small business consultative committee has raised a number of concerns in the area of small business. It has approached the present Government, concerned over the current imbalance of debt over equity in the financing of small firms and the role that the Government can play in providing an environment for entrepreneurship and investment in small business. The contribution of small business to the Canadian economy has been a large one. 1 would like to note some of these, Mr. Speaker. Some 645,000 small businesses account for 42 per cent of business employment and 25 per cent of business' Gross National Product. They demonstrate the entrepreneurial spirit and are the risk-takers to provide productivity to the economy in that some 150,000 business start-ups occurred in 1982.
There have been business failures and this is regrettable. In 1982, there were 10,765 business bankruptcies there were 410 farm bankruptcies and there were 30,463 personal bankruptcies, for a total of 41,638. In 1982, the amount of losses through business and farm bankruptcies was $2.33 billion.

Some of these people will make it back and some will not. But there are survivors-and this is the resiliency of small business.
In conclusion, the small-businessman has faced many obstacles in the path of surviving and expanding. The economic situation and policies of the federal Government have hindered the small-businessman and I would urge that the federal Government take steps to assist the small-businessman in any way it can.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note once again that the Minister responsible for this Bill always leaves the House just before I stand up to speak. I notice the former Minister responsible for small businesses is in the House so perhaps he has a greater grasp of the issue than the present Minister.
I would like to comment on a few points raised by the Minister. He indicated that this Bill ran out on March 31. The final Clause of the Bill says: "This Act shall come into force on a date to be fixed by proclamation." That does not mean it runs out on March 31, Mr. Speaker. The Minister is dreaming when he comes up with that one. He said the program was in the budget, but the budget did not mean very much because it was so far off on every number that to add another $400 million does not mean anything to this Government. I am sure they spent the $400 million somewhere else.
I am delighted to see the Minister back in the House. I would like to point out to him that I believe the 42 per cent figure he gave for small business employment is quite inaccurate. Perhaps if you include all the civil servants, all the municipal civil servants and all the other government employees in Canada, he may come close to that figure, but we are talking about the people who produce products and make this country work. Right now there are 1,600,000 people unemployed. Of that number, Mr. Speaker, over 50 per cent are from the small business sector. In addition, we have
500,000	people who have lost their jobs. In my own riding, Mr. Speaker, many former one-man businesses, "Ma and Pa" businesses, with two or three people working within the organization, are out of a job and out of Unemployment Insurance. They are "out" period. I would say, first of all- and there are statistics out on this-that the small business sector provides almost 70 per cent of the total employment. Therefore, the total of the unemployed from the small business sector is probably 70 per cent of the 1,600,000 who are unemployed. This is a very serious matter.
There is a degree of blackmail when the Minister says we must pass this Bill through the House. I cannot see our passing this Bill through the House quickly because it is not a total program. It is another band-aid used to try to patch up something after the fact. They are talking about a 12 per cent interest rate. Perhaps the banks will jump in and someone who has an interest rate of prime plus one will have it increased to prime plus five, and the banks will pick up the 4 per cent from the Government coffers. Therefore, it is a bad Act presented at
a bad time. It is not doing a real job. That is the important point, Mr. Speaker.
I do not like the "grants" approach. I find it smells of partisanship. I like economic reasons for doing something. I believe the program should be managed by the banks. They are in the front line. We in Ottawa do not know what is happening in Victoria, British Columbia, or St. John's, Newfoundland. We must have people on the scene. Furthermore, the banks this year are going to show an astronomical profit because they have recovered many losses which they anticipated and which are not going to occur. They had reserves in their books and they are going to recover those reserves. I believe the banks should participate and do their share during a period of high interest rates. They encourage people to come into the market to borrow money to expand when they need to get their money out. When all of sudden interest rates shoot up the fellow they encouraged to borrow money at the beginning is hurt because of the high interest rate policy. I believe that is totally unfair to Canadians, to small businesses, to the "Ma's and Pa's", to the fishermen and the farmers of this country.
I believe the Government is doing a bad job in trying to get out of the mess it got itself into. As an example, the Royal Bank of Canada is saying they will lease the land back to the farmer. I have had probably as much experience as anyone with the problems and hardships of people who have had their land expropriated. What happens to that land when it is tenant farmed is that the barns fall down, the houses are not painted, the land is unkept. It does not work, Mr. Speaker, to have tenant farmers. If the Royal Bank is so keen on putting the farmer back on the farm, then it should give him the farm and take lease payments against interest. Whatever the bank may get is better than what it had before, and it is much better off with an owner on that farm than a tenant because a tenant is not inclined to preserve somebody else's property.
For almost four years I have spoken about this subject, Mr. Speaker. What we need is a total, comprehensive plan for the micro, small and medium-sized industry. The SBIG is only a band-aid. It is not bad legislation, Mr. Speaker, but it does not do the job. It is not meeting the need. During severe times when interest rates go up is when we need relief, and not 4 per cent. We must give stability to our small industry. It cannot afford to go up and down with the Government interest rates, because the Government prints money to solve its problems and issues more bonds and runs into deficits. We need a secure plan to give those people in small industry the security which they require so that they can solve the one major problem we have in Canada, and that is creating jobs. It is jobs that we need. The Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Romp-key) knows that as well as anybody. He comes from an area which is in a tragic condition today. The unemployment situation in Newfoundland is serious and no one knows it better than he.
The Canadian Press wire had some very good points, one being that we need to restore a sound and lasting basis for real economic growth. But you cannot have a sound and lasting

basis with interest rates soaring and then dropping. This situation does not provide this country with any stability.
Second, we also must address, Mr. Speaker, the importance of the entrepreneurial spirit by individual Canadians. This is their country. This country does not belong to this House of Commons, nor does it belong to the civil servants who work in Ottawa. This is the country of the Canadian people and they must be given a chance to establish a lifestyle based on the entrepreneurial spirit which built this country right from the beginning. The intervention by the Government, the regulations imposed, among other points raised by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), took this away from small businessmen. They must be removed to encourage them. We must encourage youth. These youths coming out of college cannot get jobs; everyone knows that, Mr. Speaker. We must encourage them and give them the opportunity to fund their own businesses, small as they might be. For every business which is born, one out of ten will develop into something which will create numerous jobs throughout this country.
This legislation is the absolute opposite of what is needed. The Government is now trying to patch up all the tax measures which were in the budget. For instance, the 12.5 per cent on small business dividends, Mr. Speaker, is inequitable. Canadians own those businesses!
