Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-136, which is the Small Business Investment Grants Act, and on the amendments which have been put forward by the New Democratic Party.
The impact of the legislation which the Government has presented to the House is being diminished by the events which have taken place over this winter. When the business investment grant was introduced as a piece of proposed legislation, interest rates were much higher. It is necessary that the legislation the Government introduces reflect the fact that interest rates have fallen to some degree. If this legislation, which is so important to small-businessmen, is to be effective, then I think the amendments put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) must be passed by this House.
It is important to realize that there is not really that much legislation passed by this House which helps small business. One piece of legislation with which I am more familiar is the Regional Development Incentives Act. When I was the regional development critic for this Party, I found that most of the money for regional development under the RDIA was going to large businesses. In one recent year over $70 million went to businesses classified by the Government as large businesses, and $20 million went to smaller businesses. For the $70 million to large businesses, 4,690 jobs were created. For the $20 million that went to small businesses, 4,680 jobs were created. In other words, the Government of Canada spent an extra $50
Small Business Investment Grants Act
million to help large businesses and created only ten more jobs than it had with the $20 million for small businesses in this country. That demonstrates that much of Government legislation does not help small business. It also points out that small business is very important to the employment of Canadians.
A recent survey done by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business indicated that the current recession has resulted in small and medium sized businesses hiring 700,000 to 800,000 fewer people than they would have in the economic situation as it existed prior to the recession. That is 700,000 to
800,000	fewer jobs because of the recession. So when there is a Government program which is supposed to help small business, it is very important that it actually does.
The two amendments put forward by my colleague do two things. The first one allows small businesses to use this program not only for the acquisition of new equipment but for the acquisition of used equipment and the use of working capital for operating expenses. That is very important, Mr. Speaker, because 66 per cent of small businesses indicate that they are not planning expansion at the present time. Another 12 per cent indicate they will actually be reducing their production over the next little while. Those businesses are looking at economic survival. They do not want to join the 80,000 small businesses that went under last year. They want to stay in business, which means cutting operating and capital expenses. So if they can get a used cash register or scales, or other used equipment, that is a saving which might keep that business in operation. For those reasons it is important that the Government accept these amendments. I hope all Members of this House would support that.
The second amendment offered by my colleague would reduce the effective rate of interest on a loan to 10 per cent from 12 per cent. I think that is a very reasonable amendment, and it reflects the fact that when this legislation was introduced, interest rates were higher. Now, with interest rates lower, I think the Government can afford to decrease the rate so that businesses would have to pay only up to 10 per cent on a loan and still be eligible for the program. I think the Government should do this because this morning we woke up to find out that there were 1,600,000 Canadians officially unemployed in this country.
Over two million.

That means that in reality there are in excess of two million Canadians unemployed. We have heard from small business that they could be providing at least 700,000 or
800,000	jobs, so it is very important that we have legislation in place to help small business. Remember, small business provides about half of the private sector jobs in Canada. It is very important that the legislation we pass in this House actually assists those businesses, farmers and fishermen who qualify under the Act so that they can use this program to hire people, reduce the unemployment and welfare rolls in this country, and increase the purchasing power of many Canadians to get this economy moving again.

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
I am afraid that if the Government refuses to accept the NDP amendments, then this will be a hollow Act. It will not help very many Canadians. It may produce a lot of public relations, a lot of advertising by the Government as it promotes its program, but it really will not help the people it is meant to help. It will not help the small-businessmen, the farmers and fishermen who qualify. It will not help the 1.6 million unemployed Canadians. Those are very important considerations, Mr. Speaker, and I urge Government Members to support our amendments.
One of the concerns I have in the riding I represent in northern Manitoba is the fact that this Act as it is now presented allows for the purchase of new equipment only. Our amendment, which would allow the money to be used for used equipment or for operating expenses, would help many businessmen in remote communities, not just in northern Manitoba but in northern Ontario, in Atlantic Canada and in other parts of this nation. These are the businesses who have high costs because of transportation, because of their remoteness, because they tend to be dealing with smaller markets than business in communities like Toronto and Montreal. So for them new equipment is quite often out of the question. They are in a situation where they have to look around for used equipment that they can afford. When you have a potential market of only 5,000, 6,000 or 8,000 people in your community, you are not out to buy new equipment or build a new shop. You are there to try and make a few dollars to keep your family and your business going. For those businesses not to qualify under the Act as it now stands means that some of them will be going under in the future, Mr. Speaker. I urge the Government and Government Members to consider the small communities and small businesses who cannot afford new equipment. Remember them when this legislation is passed. Therefore, I urge all Members of the House to support the amendments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this discussion on Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act. I have been in the House for quite a few years and I thought I had seen a great many absurdities perpetrated by the Government, but I must say this exercise in which we are now engaged seems to outclass them all, for a number of reasons. It was pointed out this morning that this is one of the provisions of a budget that was introduced over a year ago. Of course, we are now urged to pass it quickly so that it can become effective.
As has been pointed out, this is a measure which has already become obsolete because the circumstances which existed at that time have changed and we are now faced with a totally different situation. As well, this measure fails to engage the most pressing problem, which is the need for capital at reasonable rates to assist in weathering the economic storm until the economy is stabilized and ready to move forward. I believe that, at best, the Bill in its present form would have minimal
effect and, at worse, would be completely useless. The two amendments which have been proposed and are before the House now would have some beneficial effect if they were to be included in the measure and the Bill was to become effective. As I have said before, I suggest the entire exercise is rather futile because of the economic situation having changed so dramatically since the Bill was first introduced.
For a number of reasons I consider this sector to be one of the most important in our national economy and the most deserving of consideration by the House, not just for a few minutes as suggested by the Minister but for a considerable length of time. First, it is an area of activity that provides almost unlimited scope for the expression and productive investment of individual initiative and enterprise. We are all aware of the fact that there are business and commercial enterprises in which an individual tends to become a cog in a big machine. Possibly, these large operations are essential- which I do not deny-and may be acceptable to some because of the security which they promise. However, there are many people who believe that meaning and purpose in life is found in the establishment of one's own business, farm or fishing operation, as the case may be. Perhaps it is in an area where a service is required, where one can become an integral and vital part of the community. Such entrepreneurs have usually become participants, and in many instances leaders, in the voluntary sector of those communities. Therefore, they not only render a service as far as making a living and providing employment opportunities are concerned, but also in the broader services provided by voluntary agencies.
Furthermore, we are reminded that the small and medium sized business community is the source of possibly 60 per cent of the job opportunities in this country. I believe it has been pointed out that about 42 per cent of that could be classified as small business. It is clear that the contribution that this sector has made is incalculable in terms of personal achievement, service to the community and the nation and job opportunities provided to others.
This road has never been an easy one. From the opening up of this country by venturesome individuals up to the present time, the odds have been many, their risks great and the labour tedious. In the past few years, however, the pressures have been overwhelming and these entrepreneurs have been facing insurmountable difficulties.
As has been pointed out, in 1982 a record 10,765 businesses were forced to close their doors. Business bankruptcies in 1982 were 33 per cent higher than in 1981, 63 per cent higher than in 1980 and 91 per cent higher than in 1979. This has resulted in an ever-increasing unemployment rate, as has been underlined again by the increase in unemployment figures which were just released this morning.
A recent article states that a very substantial percentage of the unemployment roll is made up of those who had previously been employed in the small business sector. In fact, one Hon. Member who participated this morning has placed that figure at approximately 50 per cent. Unemployment is increasing not
April 11, 1983

only because of an increasing labour force but by a decrease in the number of jobs available. These jobs are disappearing and while this situation remains, make-work or short-term work opportunity and programs will not solve the problems facing us.
I refer Hon. Members to the first page of the summary of a booklet put out by the Federation of Independent Business which points out that this country has not been overly solicitous to the welfare of the small business community. While the Government has outlined great programs and large projects, it has been pointed out in the article that small entrepreneurs have had great difficulty even to survive let alone make their way in their field of activity.
The provisions of Bill C-136 include the farmer and fisherman. We recently saw an example of what the Government thinks about those in the farming sector who, in order to pay their bills and keep their farms intact, take off-farm jobs. Operations are reclassified and moved into a higher tax bracket because they have the audacity to take the initiative and spend more time off the farm to make a little more money in order to pay the bills and keep the farm operating. In some instances, it means that a farmer must sell out in order to pay the taxes being imposed on his operation. It is no wonder that the Government is going down the drain.
There is a growing concern over the Government's bail-out assistance for the Domes, the Fergusons and Maislins, on the one hand, and the "sock-it-to-them" treatment of the little guy on the other. The question is: Is it less important to retain
2,000	employees in many small enterprises than to maintain one or two businesses that employ an equal number? The government's actions, I suggest, have spoken in favour of the latter.
A litany of programs and procedures has been given time and time again in response to charges that the Government is reneging on its responsibility to create and maintain an economic climate conducive to strong and virile business activity. The fact remains that Canada's economic performance has been much worse than practically all other industrialized nations in the world. Apparently there is something drastically wrong which no patchwork operation or band-aid approach will solve. It will eventually come to the point where the Government must introduce a fundamentally different approach that will effectively meet the challenges facing our business community today.
I was pleased to hear a proposal by the Minister this morning, perhaps one of the most interesting proposals he has made, that the Government is working on a strategy that seems to promise some over-all benefits to the business community. I do not know how long it will take to implement that strategy. I suggest that this current situation should constitute a shock treatment to the Government but, unfortunately, instead of taking the initiative in providing the encouragement required, it moves only when it is forced into action and only to the degree that it hopes will make it appear that something is being done.
Small Business Investment Grants Act
I appreciate the opportunity to have said a few words about the measure which is before us.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention today to put a few comments on the record regarding the Bill before us, the Small Business Investment Grants Act. I will not repeat for preservation of time some of the comments I made prior to the Easter recess when I referred to some of the banking surveys conducted by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and its suggestion that we should have a better mix of banking. For instance, the Federation related it to the experience in the United States and the relationship to commercial banks, as well as the establishment of local banks. While the risks might be higher, the concomitant effect seemed to be that at least in smaller communities there was a larger incidence of industries established in smaller communities, whereas in our situation we have the larger national chartered banks with a very extensive branch network. We have not quite had the same experience. I know there are other factors which have to be taken into consideration, but I do not have time to get into them today.
Today the unemployment figures show that 1.6 million Canadians are unemployed. In fact, that figure could be higher. I want to put that in context with an average riding, the riding I represent. I took a look at my riding just the other day. Other than one business and one federal Government operation, namely the atomic energy research facility in Whiteshell, every other business would be classified as a small business. When I talk about business in my riding, it is small business, with the exception also of Abitibi Price at Pine Falls which is a large pulp and paper operation. I want to get into that because we deal with the forestry sector as well. By the way, the best benefit which the forestry sector has had is the exchange rate, because it has been favourable for that sector in terms of export. It has not been in terms of the Canadian climate that that sector has been able to survive, it has been because of the exchange rate. I think we should be careful about what we are talking when we talk about small business. We are talking about small-businessmen and women, farmers and fishermen along the east shores of Lake Winnipeg in my riding.
What will the Bill do? I will get to the amendments in a minute, but the Bill will bring into effect a statement made in the previous budget, namely, that up to 4 per cent of interest could be reduced to a minimum of 12 per cent; or, putting it another way, for the borrower a maximum of 12 per cent. The Government will subsidize or give a grant to a maximum of 4 per cent or reduce the rate to 12 per cent. I believe the NDP amendments reduce it to 10 per cent.
My colleague who preceded me always gives us the benefit of his valuable experience. As he indicated, I wonder whether the Bill will have any effect on the small business community. The proposal was more valid at the time it was made in the budget when interest rates were obviously at levels higher than they are today. The question must be asked: Is the Bill simply

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
fulfilling the Government's promise in the budget? That might be meritorious because we have not seen the Government follow its promises in the past with that kind of keenness. In that sense I commend the Government; but will the Bill have any effect in my riding or in other ridings? The Bill indicates what one can do to be eligible. There is a $400 million ceiling, to be used for new disposable assets or financing research and development.
Last Saturday I received a telephone call from a farmer in my riding. He is trying to survive. When we talk about farmers and small business people, I guess we are talking about the most independent sector in society. They do not like to telephone their Members of Parliament and tell them that they are in trouble. It is not in the nature of these people. As was mentioned already, they are entrepreneurs and they are independent. They make their own decisions and they take their risks, but today we are receiving calls from these people. This gentleman laid out the problems he was facing as an individual farmer. Yes, he made one mistake. His mistake was that he gambled on Canada's economy and its future. That is the mistake he made. Many Canadians have made that mistake, but the difference this time is that with high interest rates he simply has difficulty surviving. In fact, this gentleman has been in farming for some period of time. I am not talking about a small farming operation. He is now on a family budget from the bank in order to retain his farm.
The Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) spoke about tenant farmers. In essence, this gentleman has become a tenant farmer on his own farm. I was shocked when he told me that last year-and I do not have the figure down to the penny as he did-he personally spent approximately $60 on clothing in 12 months. If we drive past his place, we see a farming business and good machinery. The fellow is working like many other farmers, not only from dawn to dusk but later. Not only did the figures hit me, but the fact that he said: "Jake, that I can handle. What I cannot handle is the instability and fear of the future". That is the situation which is being faced.
I respect the Minister as a person and as a Minister. I ask him whether the legislation before us really helps. Does it help this kind of person? If it helps or has the chance of helping a smidgen, it should be passed; I guess that is the rule of thumb around here. But I raise this case because I am sure every Member has similar cases in his or her riding. What are we doing for people who have been the risk-takers? Are we losing risk-takers? What I meant when I referred to them as being independent was that this man did not ask me for a grant. I found that interesting. I said: "Do you want a grant?" He had certain choice words to say about grants, but he said no. That was the essence or summary of what he said, but he wanted some kind of understanding that either a moratorium or a bank arrangement could be made which would allow him to continue farming, retain his dignity, and eventually pay his debts including interest charges. He was not asking for all kinds of forgiveness; he was asking for the opportunity to continue his operation.
I am one of the fellows in the House who argues for the marketplace. I have to ask what arrangements can be made in the public sector so that these people can continue operations outside the grant system. Let us face it, the Government is not in a position to give grants. With $30 billion of indebtedness, the Government is not in a position to give grants. All the Government is doing is borrowing to give grants. The argument is made that we should stimulate the economy even more. How much do we want to stimulate the economy-$30 billion of stimulation federally? How much provincially, another $10 billion? Can anyone on the other side guarantee that if we stimulated it by 10 per cent more we would have a better economy?
May I call it one o'clock?

In the Department of Veterans Affairs this competition takes very little account of the experience of those candidates who are actually veterans and who are in the upper age category. EFFECT OF PROPOSED CROWSNEST PASS RATE CHANGES ON PORT OF CHURCHILL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on the issue of the changes to the Crow rate and how they affect the port of Churchill. One of the rationales given for the desertion of the historic Crow rate in western Canada is that it will improve rail services in the West and help to transport more grain.
In Saturday's Free Press an official of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Doug Campbell, is reported as having told the Manitoba Legislature's standing committee that there were no plans to fix the rail track to Churchill. In addition, he said that there are no plans to prevent the shrinking of the boxcar supply in western Canada. This will result in less cars available for the transportation of grain to Churchill, Manitoba.
Since the Government has found that the only reason for changing the Crow rate is that it will improve transportation and rail services in western Canada, and given the evidence of Mr. Doug Campbell that this will not happen as far as CNR is concerned, I would ask that this House ensure that this Government does not change the Crow rate, but that it keep it there for the protection of westerners, in particular western grain shippers.

Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada is planning to change the Books of Remembrance which list the names of those who gave their lives for freedom in the Great Wars, the Korean War, and the Boer War. It is changing them to make them bilingual.
The planned procedure is to take the parchment, scrape off the ranks now in front of the names, and reprint them in the two official languages; scrape off the dates and replace them in the two official languages; scrape off the division numbers and replace them in the two official languages.
These Books of Remembrance are historical documents, and to alter them in any way is to desecrate our Canadian history. If we must have bilingual Books of Remembrance, then print duplicates, but leave these historical treasures as they were originally created.

Madam Speaker, last month the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) tabled in this House some revealing answers to my questions about the new civilian security agency. In short, the agency does not exist as yet and, I quote, "A date has yet to be fixed for the new agency to become operational".
In 1968 the Mackenzie Royal Commission on Security recommended the establishment of a new civilian agency; thirteen years later, the McDonald Royal Commission, after spending three times as much time and some 30 times as much money, came in with the same recommendation. In August, 1981, the Solicitor General announced the Government's decision to implement this recommendation and to appoint Mr. Fred Gibson as the first boss of the new service. One year later Mr. Gibson was promoted to greener pastures, and was replaced by another seasoned bureaucrat, Mr. Ted Finn.
Today there is no trace of any draft legislation pertaining to this new agency. In the meantime the operations of the RCMP Security Service suffer intolerably, in spite of the pro-forma
April 11, 1983

denials by the Solicitor General. The Government's inaction is accompanied by a discreet silence on the part of the senior security officials, although no doubt some of them will eventually step forward from the safety of their superannuated status, in the best Canadian tradition of civilian as well as uniformed mandarins. Too bad they would not do it now.
I hope, Madam Speaker, that it will not be too late for a new Government to repair the damage done to our national security by neglect and commission ever since 1968, the year in which the reorganization of our national security was first recommended and the year in which the Trudeau administration began.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL LOCKAGE FEES
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL LOCKAGE FEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to discuss an issue of considerable importance to my riding, that of lockage fees. Although all vessels using the Welland Canal are subject to lockage fees, the fee structure is designed in such a way as to effectively cause smaller boats to pay five times the rate for full-size ones. The position of the ministry on this is that the fees, which can add S3,500 to the cost of a round trip through the Canal, are needed to offset rising costs and falling revenues.
I wonder if the Minister has considered why revenues are falling? Is it because the exorbitant fees are driving many shipowners to switch to land transportation? This sounds like the classic case of the dog chasing its tail. It is a policy which defeats its own purpose. If the authorities wish revenue and usage of the Welland Canal to increase, then they should lower the fees and watch the lakers line up again to get in.
It would appear, then, that larger boats are getting preferential treatment. Why should this be the case? The smaller vessels serve ports and markets which the larger ones cannot touch. Their versatility makes up for their small size. When these ships are priced off the lakes and into the scrapyards, rest assured that the towns which depend on them will suffer. The welders who build and repair boats, the crews who work on them, and all those who rely on the Seaway for their livelihood, will be penalized as a result of the discriminatory lockage fees.
In conclusion, I would ask the Minister responsible to reexamine the lockage fees policy, in light of its harmful effects on the economy of the Great Lakes region.

The Canadian Government is spending more than $1 billion annually on training young people through its direct training programs, and that does not include the billions of dollars sent to the provinces as our contribution to postsecondary education. These amounts are being spent by the Canadian Government for the benefit of young Canadians. This year, considering the very specific problems facing young people who are about to enter the labour market, and I am thinking particularly of students, we have added another $70 million, thus raising the funding for this summer's Student Employment Program from $100 to $170 million, and recently, the Secretary of State announced an increase of $60 million for the Student Loan Program over the next two years. These are measures that were taken in recent weeks, Madam Speaker, and they clearly indicate our concern for young people and their position on the labour market at the present time, and I expect to be raising this matter again when the budget is brought down.
Before making accusations of the kind he just made, perhaps my hon. colleague would like to look at the facts and at what the Government has done in recent months, and if he does, he will realize that the Government has taken very substantial steps to try to resolve the serious problem of unemployment among young people.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Economic Development, who will know that unemployment among professional architects and engineers has reached almost 10 per cent. Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment. On a day when unemployment has reached an ever higher level the Government has issued a report on work sharing, a program which was supposed to prevent lay-offs, but the real impact of which has been to reduce people's income, including the raising of UI premiums last fall. To get on this program you have to take a lower wage, and fully 50 per cent of the people who go on the program are laid off shortly after the program ends.
Will the Minister assure this House that he will not follow the suggestion in the work-sharing report to increase unemployment insurance premiums further?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think it is important to point out that the evaluation indicated the work-sharing program has received wide support from both the users of the program and the workers in the program itself. Over 90 per cent of the workers and 80 per cent of the employers agreed with and support the program. In fact I should point out that 80 per cent of Canadians who were asked said they would approve an increase in UI premiums for the continuation of the worksharing program. That is the voice of the Canadians who are speaking to it, because they realize it is very important to save jobs and create a sense of security against lay-offs. That is exactly what work sharing has done in this country; it has provided very major protection for over 260,000 workers during this difficult period.

Madam Speaker, the Minister knows full well that the work-sharing program symbolizes the Government's approach to unemployment, which in fact is to reduce workers' income. I am shocked that he has failed to assure this House that he will not raise unemployment insurance premiums.

Madam Speaker, work sharing has reduced people's income. Going from work sharing to lay-offs reduces them further. Going onto the NEED Program reduces people's income. The policy of the Government toward unemployment has been to reduce the income of those people who continue to work. Will the Minister reject the suggestion in this work sharing report that he reduce the benefits of workers under the UIC which they have collected while on the work-sharing program? In other words, will he stop this practice of reducing the income of people who are working as his approach to unemployment?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is very sadly mistaken. The purpose of this Government is not to reduce people's income; it is to help and protect them, and give them security in the job market. If through the work-sharing program we can help avoid lay-offs, help keep people working and keep their community stable, then that will continue to be the purpose of this Government, a purpose which has obviously been broadly endorsed by all those in the program and the broad number of Canadians who were asked that question.
I did not say we would be increasing the premiums, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Finance has indicated, as have I, that we would like to maintain stability in the UI premium increase. But we must look at the new realities in the job market and take advantage of the opportunities which work sharing provides us in order to help protect workers. I am very surprised, Madam Speaker, that a Member of the NDP would be so critical of a program which has been so helpful in the protection of job security in this country.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Right Hon. Prime Minister asked us earlier to look at the reality. I realize, in considering the unemployment statistics that were released this morning, that the Government has created 29,000 new temporary jobs between October 1982 and March 1983. However, the Minister of Finance will have to admit that Canada has lost 47,000 full-time jobs.
In that case, how can the Minister of Finance, although the indicators would have us believe that an economic recovery is around the corner, how can the Minister, when he sees these figures and these statistics referring to the creation of 29,000 temporary jobs and the loss of 47,000 full-time jobs, how can the Minister still talk to Canadians about this immiment economic recovery?

Madam Speaker, perhaps my hon. colleague would like to look at the figures I mentioned earlier, which indicate that consumer confidence is now at its highest level, according to a survey by the Conference Board. Perhaps the Hon. Member would care to note that during the month of January, industrial production experienced its highest rate of growth in fifty years, and that during the same period, our gross national product experienced its highest growth rate in seven years. There are very clear indications that are apparent throughout our economy, including housing starts and increases in automobile sales, and if he

April 11, 1983
Oral Questions
looks at the figures published by Statistics Canada this morning, my hon. colleague will see that employment has increased. More specifically, over 75 per cent of the jobs created during the month of March were for adult male workers, which indicates thet there certainly has been some improvement in this area, where previous months had shown a substantial drop. I feel that from these indicators it is clear that there will be a recovery, and I hope that unemployment will drop in the months to come.

Madam Speaker, it is not the first time the Minister has said that indicators are encouraging. His predecessor also made highly encouraging predictions, but we all know how these turned out, and the Minister should realize that the Government has failed if he looks at the figures that were released. Today, since we are talking about reality, as the Prime Minister said, and more specifically, about the fact that we are losing twice as many full-time jobs as we are creating temporary jobs, could the Minister of Finance inform the House whether in a week's time, he will be able to give some indication and make some commitment with respect to the creation of full-time jobs and not just jobs that actually boil down to welfare or unemployment insurance?

Madam Speaker, I made it quite clear that in March, employment increased by 0.6 per cent, with double the average benefiting adult male workers. Nearly the entire increase in jobs for adult male workers is due to an increase in the number of full-time, not part-time jobs. Of course there is always a lag between economic recovery and job creation, as there is a lag between the orders that cause production to increase and the company's decision to hire more workers. These lags are normal and understandable.
I hope that the recovery that has now become apparent will, in the coming months, produce these new jobs, as the figures for March seem to indicate. In March, more jobs were created than in February. Unfortunately, there were also more people entering the labour market than in February, and that is why we had an increase of 0.1 per cent. It is our aim, especially through the private sector, to create as many permanent jobs as possible as quickly as possible. That is the Government's position, and I hope that the measures adopted in the budget will be along those lines and that my hon. colleague will realize that as soon as the budget is brought down next week.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. He indicated earlier that he thought that people should be more optimistic about the future of the country. I agree that the future for Canada is,
in fact, great. I am always disappointed when things do not happen.
The Minister of Finance said some time ago that structural unemployment in the future would be higher than we have been accustomed to in the past. Does the Prime Minister think that it might be appropriate to review the current income maintenance programs such as unemployment insurance and the various welfare schemes that are available, and take into account that there will be significantly larger numbers of Canadians who will be seeking employment and unable to find it, but whose needs for a stable and reasonable income will be maintained, and to bring forward some proposals which concern revamping the income maintenance programs in this country as they exist today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member raises a subject for which I have expressed concern, and I know it concerns other Ministers.
We are faced with a rather contradictory situation since some Provinces seem to be determined, at least one of them, to reduce the social benefits and social net which is available to all Canadians.
There is the problem of an aging population which is being addressed by the Government, particularly in the publication of our paper on retirement benefits. However, I think the Hon. Member correctly links the subject to the problem of structural adjustment. I want to tell him that it is a subject of concern to the Government. It is one that I addressed in my television talks last September and to which I referred again in my speech to the Liberal Convention in November, and one which the budget is very carefully examining.
Perhaps the Hon. Member's points could be expressed during the budget debate when he sees what importance we have given to the need for structural adjustment.
Madam Speaker, I think that the child who is crying in the gallery is crying for his or her future.

While reviewing the problems of employment and income maintenance, which the Prime Minister has said he is already doing, has he considered that the technological change that is occurring simultaneously with the increase in structural unemployment will undoubtedly impact the greatest on younger people?
Has he considered the possibility of shorter work weeks, and earlier retirement with a more adequate level of pension, as a means of ensuring that individuals and their families will not only be able to find employment in their younger years but will also be able to find a sufficient source of income in their older years to allow them to retire and maintain an adequate level of income and standard of living?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member asks if I have considered that. I believe I have done the same type of reading on the subject
April 11, 1983

that the Hon. Member has been doing recently. He will note that there are other ways of tackling this problem. One is to forbid overtime work to the workers, and it is not certain that we would get easy co-operation from the unions in that regard. I know that the Hon. Member would help persuade them.
Unions do not schedule overtime.

There are many avenues open to us, including some used by some countries of lowering retirement age, and increasing retirement age by other countries in order to be able to finance more easily the funds necessary for the retirement of the increased size of that segment of our population.
We are all concerned with that problem. We are all reading about it. I think it is a bit premature for me to announce any policy change. However, I repeat that we would be happy to hear from the Hon. Member during the budget debate-
Will you stay and listen?

Well, I may not stay and listen if the Hon. Member tells me that he will beat his breast. But it does not mean that his ideas will not make their way into the minds of Canadians who are always attentive to the Hon. Member's thoughts on this subject.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS WITH HIGH INTEREST RATE MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Several weeks ago the Minister of Finance suggested that he was prepared to undertake to see that Canadians who are locked into high mortgage rates would be treated in a fair and equitable fashion. CMHC has suggested that perhaps 715,000 Canadians are locked into interest rates above 17 per cent.
In the meantime a representative of one of the major lending institutions has suggested that Canadians are "SOL", simply out of luck, because there is no way they can be accommodated. Does the Minister have any specific program or plan of action to deal with this problem?

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF HOME OWNERS WITH HIGH INTEREST RATE MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have indicated that, according to the figures I have seen, most of these high rates of mortgages related to rather short terms like one year. Many of them are being renewed now at much lower rates.
In addition, there are obviously standard rules about penalties which are understandable if someone wants to get out of a
Petitions
contract into which one entered voluntarily at a particular time. It is important that those penalties not be excessive, however. I have indicated what has been the general or standard practice in that regard which I found to be reasonable.
At the same time, however, there are obviously Financial institutions which are in a situation where they are getting their funds in the form of, for instance, guaranteed income certificates that they have issued and for which some people are receiving 16, 17 and 18 per cent interest rates for five years. The same institution cannot issue a mortgage at 13 per cent and pay 17 per cent on guaranteed income certificates. As a matter of fact, this can happen in the same family. I was shown a case where a father had invested in trust company five-year certificates at 18 per cent, and his son had borrowed at 19 per cent. Now the son wants to have his mortgage at 13 per cent but the father does not want to give away the guaranteed income certificates at 18 per cent. There is a problem of balancing between the cost of money and the cost it takes to borrow that money.
