The House resumed consideration of Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 1 and 2 (Mr. Orlikow) (p. 24327).

Madam Speaker, I have just a few additional comments that I would like to place on the record regarding Bill C-136. Prior to the luncheon break, the point I was making was that small business, at least in my riding, refers to everyone conducting a business. That includes commercial enterprises and farmers.
An announcement was made today about the number of unemployed in Canada. There is no doubt in the minds of most Canadians that the best way to create employment is through the private sector. One reason I suggest we have lost as much employment and therefore have such a high rate of unemployment is that, as studies show, when businesses are asked whether they cut back-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but the time allotted to individual speakers at this stage is ten minutes and his time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I will not misuse the time the House has give to me. The point I want to make is that when small businesses were asked whether or not they have cut back on employment or have reduced employment, up to 51 per cent said that in fact they had.
In order to create employment we have got to get back confidence in that business community or sector. I say to the Government that its upcoming budget has to address that question; it cannot be done through grants. It should create a climate of confidence and give small businesses a tax regime which allows them to make a profit. They will create the jobs.
April 11, 1983

That is how we will restore the economy rather than through this program, which in fact time has already passed by in terms of its effectiveness.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the actions of the Government ever equalled its rhetoric, we would probably make some progress in the House. This Bill was introduced for first reading on October 28, 1982. It had second reading debate on Monday, November 8, 1982, and there were four speakers. Here we are on April 11, 1983, continuing report stage debate.
What has happened in the intervening five months? In November, 1982 there were 961 bankruptcies, in December there were 764, in January, 1983 there were 828, and in February, 1983 there were 978. We do not have the March figures available yet, but the projected figure is 1,028 bankruptcies in that month. If we total that up, there were approximately 4,560 bankruptcies in the five months since this Bill which was supposed to help the small business sector in some way was introduced. It is deplorable that a small six-clause Bill which is three or four pages long, with not too much in it, has had to wait so long. It is an indication of the disarray in which the Government is at the present time.
When I look at the Bill I wonder just how realistic it is today. Its purpose is to give a grant in the form of an interest abatement to certain small businesses, an abatement up to 4 per cent to reduce the interest rate paid on the acquisition of assets down to 12 per cent. Thank God bank rates have dropped in that five-month period. So the value of the Bill is somewhat questionable today.
When we look at the restraint measures which the small business community has taken, they are really staggering. Eighty-two per cent of the small businesses surveyed recently have taken restraint measures, 51 per cent have reduced the number of employees they previously employed, 30 per cent of those still employed are working with reduced hours, and 66 per cent of the companies have either reduced or postponed wage increases. Most say that in comparison with what they have done, the six and five program put in place by the Government is too generous. Their action has been one of survival.
What they need now is something to assist the equity crisis they face. They have responded to the downturn in the economy by reducing their staff, cutting inventories and cancelling capital programs. That is the classical way that a small business has to react to this sort of thing.
Now they are faced with a tremendous lack of equity funds. If you talk to most small businessmen who have managed to survive, they will tell you that their earned surplus account, which is the accumulated profits that they retained in their business over the last few years, has disappeared because they needed the funds for operating. Many of them are operating today on the good graces of their bank manager. If tomorrow
Small Business Investment Grants Act
he is a little nervous about them, they could join the ranks of those either in receivership or bankruptcy.
Aside from the difficulties of the recession and the fact that they have had to cut back their staff and inventories and cancel capital programs, they are faced with a movement in the economy. While there is not too much reduction in the number of unemployed, they see a little bit of blue sky down the road. Those I have talked to do not want to analyze where that blue sky is coming from because a cloud might cast its shadow and it will disappear. However, they feel there may be some light at the end of the tunnel.
When they look around, they feel that if they do make a profit they will be faced with a small business dividend distribution tax of 12 per cent. If they apply to buy capital assets, they still have the capital cost allowance that was included in Bill C-139. That has a disastrous effect on their cash flow. If they try to retain their employees by giving them deferred profit-sharing, that will be wiped out for new plans. They still face a great deal of difficulty in trying to operate their business.
We need an equity program. For too long the small business community has had to rely on the banks. I am not decrying the banks; they have shareholders and they have rules and regulations they have to live by. The fact is that ever since the capital gains tax was introduced, the alternate sources of equity financing for small businesses have disappeared. They have dried up. Consequently, the only place the small-businessman can get term funds today in order to operate his business is pretty well from the banks. That is one change that has to be made.
When the Minister brings down his budget on April 19, I hope he will recognize that fact. I hope he will include in the budget a provision that will allow the small business sector to acquire equity funds from other sources.
The Minister might be wise to look at what the Province of Ontario has done with the small business investment corporations. It gives a 30 per cent tax credit to people wishing to invest in small business as a small business investment corporation. There could be something along that line. A dozen different proposals have been put forward by various small business associations, such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. They put forward a number of suggestions for equity planning that will get the small-businessmen out of the banks and into another type of investment funding.
To some extent the small-businessman today is being held hostage. He has to go to his bank. The banks are faced with bankruptcy statistics. They become nervous and do not want to put their shareholders and their operations in jeopardy any more than they are at present. They become nervous and tend to keep a business on a month to month basis. The bank manager says that they will take another look at it next month or the month after. You cannot plan a business on a month to month basis. You need time, projections and many other things.
24354

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
In the past the banks have traditionally supplied short-term funds. They financed the accounts receivable, giving shortterm financing where required. In the normal course of events they were not long-term lenders or suppliers of equity funding for the small business community. That is the area we must move in.
Looking at this Bill, I would venture to say that it could have passed in one day or a day and a half had the Government put any priority on it. Five months after its introduction, we are still dealing with it today and probably will be tomorrow. It will pass and go to the Senate where it will pass in one day because they are told it is a priority Bill. It laid around for five months. Another 4,000 to 5,000 bankruptcies have been recorded by Statistics Canada in that five-month period.
I hope that some of the high-blown rhetoric the Minister used when he introduced this Bill in the first instance and some of the press releases surrounding it will translate into action. We could then go forward with other legislation which would address the problems I have mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, while this Bill means well, it is another rather feeble and consequently ineffectual attempt to help small business in a very selective way, without assessing the root cause of the difficulties affecting the whole spectrum of our economic activity. The lack of a proper economic climate, caused by the intervention and manipulative actions of this Government over the years, means that band aid measures are of doubtful value, even though I must say they are welcome.
Before proceeding further in my remarks, the attention of this honourable House ought to be directed to a very important point made by the Hon. George J. Mcllraith in the other place on Wednesday, March 30 of this year. He asked the Leader of the Government about the legitimacy of what was being done in continuing this present session without a Speech from the Throne. Personally, Mr. Speaker, like yourself, I have always had great respect for Senator Mcllraith and I believe that what he says deserves serious consideration in this Chamber. I am going to put on the record a few of the remarks which he made on that date in the other place. He said:
Honourable senators, I want to ask a question of the Government in connection with this matter.
Assuming, as appears to be possible and perhaps even probable, that the delivery of the budget on April 19 is based on the continuation of this session beyond that date, could the Leader of the Government please arrange to explain to the Senate, when it reconvenes on the afternoon of the nineteenth, by what right the government is authorized to deliver a budget for the consideration of the House of Commons without having a throne speech?
The Senator was referring to the long established practice of having a reasonable duration of time to outline the parliamentary program. One can only imagine and reflect upon the changes that have been made in the Canadian economy, partly through the intervention and manipulation of this Government since April 14, 1980, and the advisability of struggling along in the same session with this kind of change, without doing the House and the country the courtesy of bringing in a Speech from the Throne. Senator Mcllraith went on to say:
My understanding of the long-established, traditional practice-established well before Confederation and continued ever since-is that the government must submit a throne speech at the opening of a session of Parliament, and then,
when it has the vote of confidence from the House of Commons that is required-we are not involved in that procedure here-it is enabled to submit its program for the consideration of that body, and, of course, by us following upon that.
Now, we are dealing with a measure to help small business and we are all looking forward to the introduction of a budget. The whole thing in many ways seems to be putting the cart before the horse. To be dealing with select measures which, as pointed out by the last speaker, really are already partly out of date because interest rates are falling and because of other measures that are perhaps not truly indicative of what has to be done, is really an unacceptable breach of what I would consider this Parliament's sense of order and dignity to be. I just want to put this on the record because I believe that Senator Mcllraith has done the country and the House of Commons a great service in demanding some explanation from the Government Leader in the Senate for what he considers, on the basis of his long and distinguished parliamentary career, an unacceptable practice by this Government. I note that Senator Olson in the other place has promised to supply Senator Mcllraith with an answer on April 19.
Getting back to this particular measure, it is pretty obvious that it does not do very much for the average small business person. It is also clear that the goal of most small businesses today in this economic climate is to survive and not necessarily to expand. This Bill does not address the question of survival. For one thing, sir, it applies only to new equipment. Many small businesses and farmers very wisely buy used equipment. They do this for different reasons. Sometimes, as you know, sir, used equipment is of better quality and more suitable than new equipment. I have seen, as I am sure many Members of this House have seen in the past, small businesses lured by programs, whether under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or under previous programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to invest to a far greater extent than really their businesses permit because they are under the illusion that they are getting something for nothing. Therefore, they spend far more money than they had originally intended to spend. As a result, the viability of the businesses they are attempting to improve sometimes goes down the drain. Simply because the Government is so preoccupied in trying to sell new equipment, they forget the very obvious truth that there are many, many businesses in Canada which have large inventories of used equipment which they would be very happy to sell and which in some cases, as I say, would be far more suitable to the aspiring business people who want to use them than the more expensive and sometimes inferior new equipment.
This Bill is also very vague and provides for far too much discretion to be granted to the Governor in Council to make regulations concerning the operation of the program. The only details specified in the Bill are the 12 per cent ceiling and the 4 per cent maximum grant. Also, the right of the Government to
April 11, 1983

get back money that was granted to those not entitled to the money is there, and the authority to make these regulations is there. My colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is proposing an amendment that would require parliamentary approval of all Orders in Council governing the operation of the program. It seems to me that this is a far more advantageous way to go about it than to leave so much uncontrolled discretion in the hands of the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that while we are waiting for the budget to come in and hoping that the Government will have done something for a change to encourage Canadian businesses, we should look at ways to do something far more imaginative to help small businesses than is encompassed in this rudimentary and very unimaginative piece of legislation.
In the United States of America, I think there are 17 or 18 duty-free ports. Just imagine, with a little bit of initiative, what we can do with a duty-free zone in Nova Scotia, one in New Brunswick and one on the West Coast, where we could establish assembly plants, and also use some of the techniques that the Americans have used with their DISK program. We could export these components, the parts of which we could bring in duty-free. We would not sell them domestically, of course, but we could export them to countries which in many instances would be only too pleased to buy them and it would improve our balance of trade. But this Government does not seem to be interested in taking any fundamental initiatives. It has the idea that you can just continue to put forward band-aid approaches and subsidize people, tell them what to do and manipulate them and hope that something will happen that will cause things to improve.
This Government and the Liberal Party have come a long way from the days when they followed the advice of Adam Smith, when they believed in free enterprise and individualism, when they believed in reform. Now, they have gotten the whole spectrum of our economy so tangled with their interventionist and manipulative strategies and their suffocating regulations that they have defeated the very purposes for which they once stood. This Bill does nothing really except provide some filler for the House of Commons to debate and raise a very few hopes in a carefully selected and very narrow area of business without really addressing some of the causes or offering much hope.
My colleague who just spoke pointed out that it is the banks which are the primary source of funds and they still require a tremendous amount of extra collateral and security for small business. There is nothing in this legislation or in any legislation to help or encourage banks to be a little bit more forthcoming with the kinds of collateral requirement that they need.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you know many businessmen in your constituency who are sound, who are well set up and financed, and yet whose houses and businesses and inventories are covered by some sort of floating charge or mortgage that really constricts these people if they want to take a chance and get into some kind of related enterprise based on their own good training and business experience.
I do not understand why the Canadian banks are so preoccupied with covering their collateral again and again rather
Small Business Investment Grants Act
than allowing businessmen to have a little bit of flexibility, particularly when they have built up a good track record. The history of our country is just full of instances where, because of the ultra-cautious nature of Canadian banks and the shortsighted policies of various Governments in the past, Canadians have had to go abroad to develop and prosper. I know of one instance where a prominent businessman was asking a major Canadian bank to finance his initiatives in offshore oil development. The bank studied his proposal and they said to him: "Yes, sir, we will, but you will have to sell your house in Canada and establish a residence in Bermuda, and you will have to do it offshore. On that basis, we will finance you."
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how you feel about it but as a Canadian it makes me sick to see the kind of evasions and manoeuvres that have to be taken by a Canadian who wants to get involved in developing his own country but has to go offshore, with the co-operation of Canadian banks, to do it because of the unimaginative tax policies and the business constrictions that this Government keeps imposing.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak this afternoon on the Small Business Investment Grants Act. It provides for an interest grant of up to 4 per cent per annum for two years to be paid to lending institutions on behalf of the borrower by the federal Government on loans made to eligible small businesses for specified purposes.
This temporary program, which has a ceiling of up to $400 million, is designed to reduce the cost of borrowing for the acquisition of certain new depreciable assets or for the financing of research and development.
I think the foregoing is the key to the Act and is important when discussing the amendments we have offered. The Bill was placed before the House in October 1982, when it was sorely needed.
Our first amendment would have the effect of allowing the grants to be applied to loans for operating expenses and other requirements. The second amendment would reduce the interest rate to 10 per cent, rather than 12 per cent. These two amendments were placed before the House on November 23, 1982, when they were sorely needed to help small business to survive. They are needed even more today.
At the present time, in April of 1983, 5,000 bankruptcies later, the need for the Bill has been reduced considerably. A lot of small businesses and farms have already gone down the drain. The need has also been reduced considerably because interest rates have come down. Instead of the 4 per cent reduction provided in the Bill, 2 or 3 per cent would probably be sufficient. Very few of the businesses that are still around hope or intend to expand.
There is still a need for our amendments, however. The events that have occurred in the economy since last October prove the validity of those amendments. The money is not

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
needed for expansion but for survival, and therefore should be provided to the small businesses at a rate as low as is possible.
What we have here is another case of the Government failing to act when action was needed. Now it is ready to act when the cost will be less. But even if the Government decides to act now, it has not taken cognizance of its own research and studies which have cost the taxpayer two years of time and approximately $2 million. This was the cost of the small business financing review which indicated the need for financing small businesses and the need for lower interest rates if they are to survive.
The Government assures us that the Bill will solve the problem of small business. It has not defined the problem as survival, however, but only as expansion or research. If the problem is survival, let us remember that during this recession small and medium-sized businesses have released 700,000 or
800,000	employees. That is a major portion of the number of unemployed people in the country. The Government offers small business slightly reduced interest rates for expansion and research and, by those terms, has excluded over 66 per cent of the small businesses which may need money but cannot get it at a reasonable rate as things stand. These figures come from a survey conducted by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
The amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) would provide money at a more reasonable rate. The philosophy behind this kind of assistance needs to be examined. For instance, in Saskatchewan a Tory Government has been in office for one year. Recent Statistics Canada figures show that in Saskatchewan there are now 40,000 registered unemployed people. That is not counting the 12,000 who have returned to the farm and claim that they are farming. It is an increase of 14,000 people over the number unemployed a year ago, or a jump of 54 per cent in one year. This is the situation in a Province where the Government promised to bring the children home to good jobs and prosperity.
Other Provinces have not fared quite so badly, but the Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the federal Government are adopting the same kind of philosophy-to help out the big corporations by reducing royalties and inviting them to invest, while giving very little important help to small business, farmers and fishermen. They are given only token support, Mr. Speaker.
That is exactly what this Bill offers-token support in an area where more than 66 per cent of businesses cannot use it. Unless the Government accepts our amendments, the value of the Bill is negligible. Why is it that when the Government claims it is going to do something for small business or to assist people, it throws in conditions which make it impossible for them to take advantage of the offer?
For instance, over the last year there have been a number of programs designed to help people in dire straits. However, if a small businessman wants to apply for a Small Business Bond, a bank can claim that he is not a good risk and refuse to lend the money. If he is not in dire straits and the bank would lend him the money, then the Government says it would not advance
money because he is not in dire straits. Obviously, if the bank would lend him money, he is not in a bad enough condition to need the money.
Until a few months ago, farmers who tried to get money from the Farm Credit Corporation faced the same dilemma. If they were not in dire straits they could not get money; if they were in dire straits, they could not get the money because they were not considered a good risk.
Could it possibly be that the Government is incompetent? Let us hope that if the Bill passes with our amendments, it will work well to support small businesses through the recession.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a nation of small business. There are well over 1 million such enterprises in the country. They are the lifeblood of the nation and employ in the vicinity of 2.5 to 3 million Canadians. That is approximately one-fifth of the labour force.
These businesses account for something like 25 per cent of the Gross National Product, so when the Canadian small business sector thrives, the whole country thrives; when the small business sector falls upon hard times, so do hundreds of thousands of individual Canadians. That is what we see at the present time. In fact, it is what we have seen for the past couple of years. No sector of our society has been hit harder by recent ill-conceived and ill-timed economic policies initiated by the Government than has the small business sector.
I say that because I think it is unfortunate that this has happened. The Government, having no consideration for this sector, having no forethought about what might happen, did not foresee the blows it would hammer upon the small businesses of this country. Its misguided high interest rate and its disastrous budget of November, 1981 dealt devastating blows to the small business sector of this country. About 80,000 small businesses have either gone into bankruptcy, into receivership or into insolvency as a result of these measures, Mr. Speaker.
Just recently the Canadian Federation of Independent Business carried out a survey on what kind of impact these measures have had on the small business sector. They found that roughly three-quarters of a million Canadians-roughly one-half of the total of those who are out looking for work today-were laid off by small and medium sized businesses in the last year. That was reported, Sir, in the Ottawa Citizen of March 23, when the details of their survey were released. In The Globe and Mail business supplement of March 25 there was further comment about the survey which had been carried out by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. They had this to say, and I quote:
The survey showed that 51 per cent of the responding businesses had reduced the number of their employees since early 1981. Few had plans for increasing hiring or investment. Nationally, 66.7 per cent expect to retain present employment levels, 9.1 per cent would be rehiring laid-off workers, and only 7.9 per cent would be hiring additional people.
April 11, 1983

The picture on investment intentions was similar: 61.2 per cent planned no change, 8.8 per cent planned to bring investment back to pre-recession levels,
11.2 per cent planned decreases, and only 11 per cent planned increases.
In other words, Sir, what the Canadian Federation of Independent Business was able to establish very clearly from the data of this survey was a reflection of the doubts and suspicions which the business sector has toward this Government, doubts and suspicions, which, I may say, are very well founded. I have talked to a great many business people, both in my own riding and elsewhere in the country, about their concerns, about the pressures and the tensions and the worries to which they have been subjected as a direct result of this Government's high interest rates policies, of the reluctance of the chartered banks to provide any kind of relief to those who find themselves in difficulty, and of the continuing uncertainty which they face as to what blows the Government will be aiming in their direction next.
The budget of November, 1981 and its regressive tax measures has deeply scarred the business community of this country, not just businesses as such, not just the business sector, but the individuals who work within that sector. The budget of June, 1982 followed. It did very little to reassure the small business community that this Government knew where it was going. Oh, yes, it did impose a six and five restraint program on certain Government spending programs, but really that was nothing compared with the restraint which the small business sector had already disciplined itself to abide by.
The Bill which we have before us today, Sir, Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act, comes out of the budget of June of last year which I mentioned. Anything which proposes to improve the position of small business operators in this country is welcome and, indeed, this piece of legislation is welcome, but in reality it will have very little impact. It offers a 4 per cent reduction in interest rates for the acquisition of certain new depreciable assets or for the financing of research and development, but it applies only to grants which are above a 12 per cent interest rate floor. It does not apply to used equipment and, as my colleagues on this side of the House have said, so many small businesses deal in used equipment. They do not always want to lay out the cost of new pieces of machinery. It also does not deal with the needs of businesses which are desperately in need of funds simply to survive.
One can say, I suppose, that this Bill is designed to encourage expansion, but if that is the case, Sir, it underlines very clearly the fact that it would have done absolutely nothing for the 80,000 businesses which went bankrupt or which went into receivership in the last couple of years. Nor will it really be of any help to the great majority of businesses which are unable to contemplate any expansion in the next year. As the survey of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business shows, they are not planning or contemplating any expansion, they are hoping just to be able to retain the status quo. Of course, these businesses, or the great majority of them, will not be able to avail themselves of this particular piece of legislation.
One of its major deficiencies, as has been pointed out on a number of occasions, is that this Bill makes it mandatory that
Small Business Investment Grants Act
much of the operation under its legislation will be carried out by as yet unknown Government regulations and by Orders in Council. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), has addressed himself to this very issue, that is, the ongoing tendency of Government to do everything in secret. He addressed himself to this particular aspect of the Bill by putting forward an amendment which would require Parliamentary approval for all Orders in Council governing the operation of the program, and that, Sir, is a much needed improvement to the Bill. I hope the Government has taken very clear note of it and that it will accept the proposal which my colleague has put forward.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business has declared that more confidence in Government policy and consistency is really necessary before a full recovery of the economy can begin. Nothing is more important, Sir, than that we have a climate and environment in which the business sector can flourish. Certainly, if that were to be so-and it is not so at the present time-no group would avail themselves more of opportunities to develop and to expand than would the small business sector.
It was very interesting to look at this morning's insert in The Globe and Mail. Their complete report on business referred or directed itself to small business only, and the major headline read, "Independent Entrepreneurs are a Developing Force". Well, they have been a force in this country throughout its history, and they will continue to be a force if the climate and environment permit them.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that we on this side of the House are not only urging the Government but praying that the Government help provide that climate and that environment when the long awaited budget of next Tuesday is brought forward.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, as in so many instances in this Government's programs, this Bill addresses only part of the requirement of small business. It is to be hoped, of course, that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) brings in his budget, he might then address the balance of the problem, and I would like to address part of that problem this afternoon.
The tax structure of this country has mitigated against the family business, whether it be the farmer, the garage man, the manufacturer or the fisherman. It started out, of course, with the inheritance tax. Later came the capital gains tax. Now we have the reduction in the capital goods depreciation allowance. As a result of these moves, the little business guy has found himself in considerable difficulty in attempting to perpetuate his business. Small businessmen are the backbone of their communities, big or small. To supplement the figures of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) let me say that when you include the farmer, fisherman, the serviceman and small manufacturer, you find that small business provides between 60 per cent and 70 per cent of the total employment in Canada. I do not contradict her figure

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
of 25 per cent because I think that refers primarily to businesses other than those in the primary sector. I merely supplement what she has said. I wish to address those facts to the Minister responsible for this Bill as well as to the Minister about to be responsible for a new budget, because small business must be given some consideration.
I can well remember Mr. Lewis, the Leader of the New Democratic Party, referring to "corporate welfare bums". He said that they were leaning on the Government for subsidies and assistance of one kind or another. Let me point out that they did not, either then or now, get into that position through their own choice. They are there because of the burden of taxation imposed upon them. That is why they fell into that category so aptly described by Mr. Lewis. When are we going to get to the point where there is an incentive for business, small or large, to produce and employ? When are we going to realize that overtaxation creates unemployment? When are we going to realize that by reducing taxes we assist in the accumulation of working capital and stimulate demand which, in turn, will cause business to expand production and employment? We have long since reached the point of diminishing returns through taxation. Until we address that problem, all the Supplementary Estimates and legislation we may introduce are not going to succeed.
Under the current economic situation this kind of legislation should be compulsory. It does in fact lend some help to small business in all spheres of activity. But, again, it is dependent upon the public purse for assistance, which then entails regulation and interference in the small business world.
I accept the fact that there is an element of urgency in this Bill, because my constituency has a multitude of fishermen and farmers who have not been eligible for Government benefits. Therefore, I subscribe to the idea that this Bill should go through, but I also subscribe to the idea that it only partially addresses the probem. When we talk about tax consideration for individuals, not necessarily incentives but a reduction in taxes, this is the greatest stimulator of employment. If small businesses had a more favourable tax structure, how many thousands more would they employ? Yes, they might not pay as much to the Government, but then how much less would the Government be paying out? How many hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent in Government programs to provide temporary employment, and how many tens of millions of dollars might be spent to stimulate employment in the small business area, employment which is so badly required in this country? For example, our Party recently released an agricultural program in which it agreed that there should be a tax consideration for that industry of not less than 20 cents per gallon of gasoline. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this tax reduction would make a major contribution to the farming industry. When this Government decided it should tax gasoline to the extent of roughly 80 cents per gallon, it imposed on the farmer, fisherman and forester a massive increment in costs. Then we turn around and pass a Bill which will pay grants to those same people who, if they could get tax considerations from this Government instead of tax punishment, would
probably never use this legislation unless it were to create much greater employment.
How badly has the Government interfered in these spheres of endeavour? Well, let us first discuss the fishermen. In the fishing industry, we have interfered in licensing, in the qualifications of people who, in many instances have been in the industry for 10 to 40 years. They are told they are not fishermen, they should not have a licence, they cannot get a new licence. However, if they get a licence, the size of their boat is regulated, and after that the size of their catch is regulated. In other words, the fishing industry is strangulated by regulation.
With regard to the forest industry, we recently had a new commission appointed, which has in turn been placed under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley). It is another fragmentation of the administrative function of this Government. It is rather interesting to note that in the makeup of that commission, which is to study the forest industry in some fashion or other not particularly clear to me from the news release, there is not a single member of the Department of Forestry of the Government of Canada who is to be present at meetings and therefore who will be cognizant of the statements which will be made for the betterment of the industry. It just cannot be, Mr. Speaker, that we should have under Industry, Trade and Commerce a committee which is going to make recommendations with respect to the forest industry when we already have a Minister who is responsible for forestry. This does not make much sense.
When are we going to recognize the requirements of the small-businessman in the forest industry? When are we going to return to him the tax structure under which he developed his industry and without which he probably cannot continue to function? When are we going to extend to these primary industries those things which would eliminate the necessity for grants and create the opportunity for employment so badly needed?

Mr. Speaker, once again I see it is only Members of our Party who are rising to speak on behalf of small business in this country. No one on the Government side or the NDP side is rising. That is typical, Mr. Speaker, because this is another Bill which does not really do much for the small business community. The Government makes announcements across the country: "Look, folks, we are doing this, and this and this", and yet it is five months since the Bill was brought forward, and the Government has not given it any priority at all. In the meantime, hundreds of companies, which means men and women like you and me, Mr. Speaker, have lost a fortune because of broad Government policies which have bankrupted the nation as a whole.
I know the Bill is going to mean an interest abatement of some 4 per cent to bring the real interest rate on loans to 12 per cent, but that is not really going to help most companies these days because it does not really address the fundamental
April 11, 1983

problem affecting small business across this country, that of a loss of confidence. It is a loss of a good business climate so that men and women will not even invest their dollars and take a chance on a small grocery store. Why could anyone put his or her money into a venture like that and work 18 hours to 20 hours a day when they will simply be taxed and hounded to death by regulations at both the federal and provincial level?
That brings me to the major point I want to make in the ten minutes that I have. The unseen battle which has been occurring in this country of which most people are not aware is the federal-provincial battle over tax jurisdiction. This battle has meant that ordinary Canadians, and small businessmen in particular, have been hurt. This battle relates to the enormous growth of Government since the Second World War, and certainly during the last 15 years under this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal Government.
There are over 400 federal Crown corporations. Those Crown corporations have subsidiary corporations and subsubsidiary corporations. As well, the Provinces have Crown corporations with similar subsidiaries. The federal-provincial battle has ensued in this area because there is no cross taxation between the different levels of Government. When the federal Government establishes a Crown corporation that is not subject to real provincial tax, the provinces respond by setting up their own Crown corporations. The over-all result is that the tax base has been reduced so that individuals are paying an enormously enhanced rate of tax to enable the federal Government to raise the $88.9 billion that it needs. We know that it will only raise approximately $50 billion since its yearly deficit for which it will have to borrow is over $30 billion.
Part of the solution to this problem is to create a business climate in which there is a proper balance between the federal and provincial Crown corporations. I argue that they should be forced to operate in the marketplace and pay their fair share of taxes, rather than escaping them and having them foisted on individual Canadians and small-businessmen. Naturally, I would prefer to see far fewer Crown corporations and more genuine private enterprises conducting these businesses presently run by Crown corporations. I believe in this approach because when Crown corporations are established and are made responsible to a certain Minister, that Minister will assume the responsibility for that corporation. Therefore, it will succeed if it takes every tax dollar and every subsidy that can possibly be obtained since it is a reflection on the Government if it fails. Therefore, whenever any of these 400 federal Crown corporations experience difficulty, they simply go back to the public purse and they are protected by various means, including a direct influx of tax revenue.
An example of this is Petro-Canada. There was $6 billion or $7 billion of national wealth poured into that corporation, not for it to create anything new, but simply to buy existing corporations which were paying taxes. Is Petro-Canada paying tax? While they may funnel in a few dollars each year, when one looks at the Estimates it can be seen that Petro-Canada receives again this year almost $400 million in spite of the fact that even the dummies in the oil industry have been making
Small Business Investment Grants Act
profits and paying taxes to the nation. Petro-Canada is still into our pockets and we are facing a lower standard of living in order for that corporation to succeed, because it is ours. So the first step should be to create a proper balance between private enterprise and Crown corporations.
Another drawback of Crown corporations is their size. Normally, when a new technology emerges, there are dozens of corporations and individuals who are competing for that technology. Once an individual or corporation secures that technology and adapts it, it then becomes the normal mode of operation for that particular industry. Although some corporations go bankrupt in the process, they are small and those who are employed in those corporations can easily be absorbed elsewhere. However, when a Crown corporation is established, it becomes larger and larger. It cannot face failure because tens of thousands of people are put out of work and must fall back on Unemployment Insurance. As a result, a greater amount of our tax revenue is poured into the corporation even though the technology has changed.
I will cite a classic example of this technological change, one which will never be permitted to happen again. Only a few years ago there were service stations on practically every street corner, and on the four corners in certain areas. Due to the technological change in cars, the industry was forced to adapt and to reduce to approximately a quarter of its original size. Since these service stations were owned by private individuals and competing corporations, a reduction process was evolved and self-serve stations were established.
Would this change have been permitted to occur if they were all Petro-Canada stations which were owned by the state as a whole? Of course it would not because the Crown corporation would have been able to come to us, politicians, and since it was a state-trading corporation which could not be allowed to fail, we would have had to kick in a large amount of tax dollars.
Another example concerns CNR for which we have to write off over $800 million every few years. Air Canada has to be given all kinds of special and privileged regulatory positions such as monopoly lines. As well, it receives low interest bonds. I recently read its annual report which indicates that Air Canada still has some bonds outstanding at 5 per cent interest. That is an enormous subsidy which we do not get as individuals when we go out to borrow. But our Government is not helping us a bit.
It is evident therefore, that the tax base has injured us rather dramatically. I wish to talk about the solution because the real solution lies in the business climate. There are two practical steps the Government could take to help the small business with which I deal mostly, that is, the farming community. It concerns gas taxes. Since the introduction of the National Energy Program approximately six new gas taxes have been levied on a gallon of gasoline. In western Canada particularly there are millions and millions of acres which have to be traversed at least five times a year. In the spring the

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
farmer must go over the land to prepare his seed bed, then go over it once again to seed. He then must go over it to spray chemicals, and often once again to spread fertilizer. The land must then be swathed in the fall, then harvested, and finally gone over again in before the winter. In my Province of Alberta, the federal taxes and royalties are almost 60 per cent of the price of that gallon of gasoline. If the federal Government wished immediately to help small business, it could remove that 9 per cent sales tax, which would represent 20 cents on a gallon of gas. This would be an enormous help to small business in that area.
A second major step would be to abolish the capital gains tax. As we know from our past discussions here, the increase in value of farmland and small businesses has nothing to do with real gain. It is solely the result of inflation, which we know is the result of deficits, which in turn lead to inflation, high interest rates and ultimately to a collapse. I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) did not mean to mislead the House when he suggested that the NDP was not putting up speakers. We had a speaker from Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) and another one from Churchill (Mr. Murphy).

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking at report stage of Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act, let me begin by saying that it is very difficult to develop a critique of the legislative provisions contained in this Bill in the short time that is available to us.
It should be pointed out that these provisions are largely academic. They were brought forward to the House of Commons in the form of Bill C-136 at a time when interest rates were much higher than they are today. Therefore, the measures that were intended to benefit small-businessmen might be largely lost as a result of a reduction in interest rates. Hopefully, those small businesses which are now seeking to borrow funds for investment purposes will find an available interest rate that is not too far above the minimum permitted by this Bill, namely 12 per cent. Nevertheless, what is important is the spirit that, hopefully, is evident in the provisions of Bill C-136. That spirit is an indication that the Government is finally looking toward that sector of the economy known as the small-business community to build for the future. It goes without saying that those of us who embrace the Progressive Conservative Party philosophy of support for small business welcome any measure which will encourage the small-business community in Canada.
It is difficult to develop any particular theory with respect to the development of small businesses in Canada over the next decade, in the time available, but let me begin by considering what is the greatest economic problem in Canada today, that is, unemployment. We learned today that unemployment has
again risen to a level of 1.6 million unemployed Canadians and a rate of 12.6 per cent. That is only part of the story because, in addition to the many thousands who are unemployed, there are those Canadians who have given up looking for work and those Canadians who are employed at jobs much below their level of qualification or employed only part-time. When we put all those numbers together, we have over three million Canadians with an employment problem. I want to look at this great economic problem in relation to the small-business community.
We must be aware, as other speakers have pointed out, that the Canadian small-business community accounts for employment of almost 42 per cent of the working force. When we include in that statistic medium-size businesses, the percentage of persons employed in Canada rises to 66 per cent. If we are looking for a method of relieving the unemployment problem, which as I said is our greatest economic concern, then we are right to look to the small and medium businesses across Canada to relieve that problem and to create the employment necessary to eliminate or at least minimize the problem.
In order to find answers to what will help the small-business community generate the jobs which will allow us to reduce our unemployment problem, we should consult with persons engaged in the operation of small businesses. It is interesting to note that organizations like the Canadian organization of small businesses and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business have looked at all these problems and have made presentations which in part provide answers to the question of how we in the Parliament of Canada can help small business in its future undertakings. Basically it comes down to the fact that we have to advocate and embrace in our economic system the principle of free enterprise. We have to acknowledge that it is essential in Government, as in business, to balance the budget, that is to say, to relate Government expenditures to Government income to ensure that there is not a drain on the financial resources of the private sector in Canada.
This means that in endorsing these principles we will create an atmosphere in Canada which will be conducive not only to small businesses but to business activities at all levels. That is the first message which these organizations bring to Parliamentarians: that we must embrace the principle of free enterprise and recognize the economic fact of the necessity of a balanced budget. If we adhere to those principles, we will create an atmosphere in which it is possible for small businesses to be established and to succeed. As one Member of Parliament I want to endorse those principles and to ask and beseech the Government to give full recognition to them when it establishes its economic policy in its forthcoming budget.
The importance of establishing those principles is that they are far-reaching. They mean that a person who makes the effort to invest in and to establish a business or a business activity has a right to the profits of that business or activity and that profit ought not to be taken away by a taxation system which deprives a business person of the incentive to establish a business and to carry it on even through difficult
April 11, 1983

times. When we talk about basic principles, we must recognize at the same time that they have far-reaching results.
There is an aspect which business organizations representing small-business operators across Canada bring to Parliament which I would like to underline-they fully recognize their ability to create jobs in Canada. Let me give the downside of that statement, because the Canadian Federation of Independent Business reported that in the year which elapsed between January 1981 and January 1982 there was a loss of between
700.000	and 800,000 jobs in the small and medium business sector. This gives us an idea of how this small-business sector reflects on the over-all picture with respect to unemployment and in turn the over-all status of the Canadian economy.
What can we do to help small business reverse that trend and not have a job loss in its activities in the country but have job creation throughout its activities? It is very clear-and we have been told time and time again-that the Government has to provide financial assistance to start small businesses in Canada. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business pointed out, in a presentation which was provided to Members of Parliament, that notwithstanding the difficult times we have experienced in Canada in the last few years, small-business operators have continually come forward as entrepreneurs to start new businesses. In fact, in 1982 there were 150,000 formulations. This organization pointed out that with a potential upturn in the economy in 1983 we could expect some
200.000	formulations, that is, entrepreneurs across Canada who will attempt to start small businesses. Also it was pointed out by the Federation that if these 200,000 formulations were to start up and in each case hired one or two persons, as many as 400,000 jobs would be created.
What is necessary and required from Government to encourage the start of small-business formulations is financing. It is as simple as that. Does the Government have the ability to provide financing for small-business start-ups? That is a difficult question. We are looking at a Government which has piled up a budget deficit of some $30 billion. That in itself has made difficulties for business because it raises the rate at which one can borrow funds for business purposes from every lending institution across Canada.
My answer to that is a very simple one. We cannot afford to deprive small businesses of the kind of financial assistance they need to start because if we deprive small-business operators of that financial assistance, we will simply sink into the abyss of economic depression. We have to build and rebuild the Canadian economy. We have no choice. Our only choice is to do it with the co-operation of small business.
We have seen in the House of Commons and across Canada in the past year or two the collapse of project after project, such as the Alberta tar sands project which would have employed 10,000 people directly and many more indirectly. On the East Coast we see offshore development failing to yield the kinds of jobs we thought would be yielded through energy developments in the 1980s. While I would not negate the possibility of large scale development across Canada, the hard economic fact is that we have to look to small and medium size businesses to create activities which will generate jobs and
Small Business Investment Grants Act
correct the unemployment problem in Canada. If financial assistance is needed to start these businesses, that is what the Government of Canada must provide.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-136 and the amendments we are discussing at the present time. I, as I would imagine a number of Members of Parliament who do not have suntans, have spent most of the holiday in my constituency visiting small businesses and those who are experiencing certain problems in today's economy. The small-business sector is one which is extremely hard hit by what we are going through at the present time. Probably the greatest single deterrent to small businesses today is the fact that they lack confidence. They lack confidence in the Government. They lack confidence in the economy. In many instances they lack confidence in themselves because of the position in which they have been put over the last number of years, specifically in the last couple of years, by this Government. Some of these businesses have money to invest, expand and hire more people, but they do not trust the present administration. They have a very real concern.
The question they ask me is what the Government is going to do to them next. They want to know what rules are going to be changed next in the middle of the game. Confidence will not be restored unless on April 19 we have a commitment from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Government, as much as that will be worth, to leave the small business sector alone. They want to be promised that the tax regime now in place will not change and that the rules of the game will not be changed part way through without proper notification and consultation. Right now they are gun shy of this Government after the three budgets that came forward in a year and a half. I believe there have been 65 or 70 changes since the infamous budget of the then Minister of Finance, now Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen).
Small businessmen want to be assured that the rules of the game will not be changed come April 19, 1983, 1984 or 1985. If they had this assurance, they would be prepared to invest and expand. I am hearing far too much about those looking south of the border to invest. They are being invited to expand in that country, to set up a plant or move their operation to the United States where they will receive certain guarantees that there will be no interference in their business.
This bothers me. It concerns me greatly. I have to hear businesses or individuals talk about leaving this country or moving their business elsewhere. The April 19 budget must restore some of that confidence to Canadian businesses, especially small businesses which are the backbone of our economy, which hire the people and produce for Canadians.
I now want to talk about the amendment of my colleague from the New Democratic Party. The Act now clearly states that these loans can only be made for new depreciable assets or

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
for the financing of research and development. As I travel around the communities of Brampton and Georgetown, I see more and more vacancies in plants and small operations in the industrial sections of the community. For the life of me I cannot understand why these loans would not be available there.
I questioned the Minister as to why these loans were not available for older, second-hand, used equipment as well as for buildings. I know they are not eligible for land, but they are for buildings. I asked why these moneys were not approved under this program for used buildings. I cannot see the sense of erecting new buildings to take advantage of a plan like this when there are so many vacant buildings across this country. Therefore I, along with my colleagues, support the amendment brought in by our colleague. I urge everyone to support that amendment.
I now want to talk about the closing date of this program. It is not mentioned in the legislation, but the regulations state that this Act is null and void as of April 1, 1983. It is now April 11, 1983, so we are debating a Bill that has run out of steam. We are talking about a few loans that must be made to those who have applied and are waiting to receive them. We will not hold those loans up unduly.
This Government continues to say that the Opposition holds up this type of legislation when it in fact controls the timetable of this House. To blame that on the Opposition Parties is heresy. It is completely untrue. This Bill could have been put through well before Christmas and the loans made. There is no excuse whatsoever for debating a Bill that has run out of time. It is after the fact.
We will be introducing an amendment later that I hope will be supported by this House. If the Bill were to be passed as it is now, it would not serve any real purpose. On loans to small businesses, they cannot charge any more than 1 per cent above prime. Prime is now 11.5 per cent. Therefore, loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act would be at 12.5 per cent. This Act, with all the bureaucracy, forms to be filled out and everything else, would not make much sense. It would be much smarter to go under the Small Business Loans Act.
We understand that the applications that are before the Minister and have not been approved must be approved. We support that. Now that interest rates have dropped, this Bill will not have any real effect. It will be a duplication of the Small Businesses Loans Act.
I am sure the Minister has received input into his April 19 budget. I encourage him to give confidence to the business community, especially the small business community. Let him assure them that the rules of the game will not be changed when they are part way through trying to expand, trying to create employment and getting Canada back on the road to recovery.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to take part in this debate on Bill C-136, the Small Business Investment Grants Act, as it applies to operators of small businesses in Canada. It has been widely
ascertained that neither the federal nor provincial Governments have ever agreed upon or accepted an economic definition of small business. What is more amazing is that people all across Canada who profess to be proponents of small business have not agreed on a clear definition either.
When talking about the size of business, Governments emphasize the size of assets, the size of sales, the number of employees and so on. I believe that size is less important in defining small business than many other factors. I believe that small is a relative term. What is small in one industry could be termed medium or large in another sector.
I believe that a small business definition is one in which a business is independently owned and managed and has at the most 500 employees. This definition of a small business is the law in the United States, and many other countries around the world have adopted it. The 65,000-member Canadian Federation of Business, the largest business organization in Canada, has also adopted this definition.
This Government, on the other hand, has not been able to reach a consensus on a general definition. The Government has resisted the concept of owner-management, preferring to use a much more vague one which allows employee-managed plants to be classified as small businesses. Hopefully this problem will be resolved in the near future to the satisfaction of everyone concerned.
The substance of Bill C-136 will provide the necessary legislation to implement the Small Business Investment Grants Program outlined in the June, 1982 budget. This program, as we already know, will provide grants of up to 4 per cent to reduce interest costs to as low as 12 per cent. This Bill also has a ceiling of up to $400 million and is designed to reduce the cost of borrowing for the acquisition of new depreciable assets or for the financing of research and development. Those eligible to receive such a loan include farmers and fishermen, small businesses and corporations eligible for the low corporate tax rate, and also partnerships and proprietorships. However, those engaged in a profession or those wishing a loan for the purchase of land, automobiles and certain other passenger vehicles and leasing do not qualify for such loans. In order to qualify for a small business investment grant, a loan application must be for an amount not less than $10,000 or greater than $500,000.
One of the problems with Bill C-136 is that since this Bill was first considered about six months ago, the interest rates have fallen to the point where the 12 per cent ceiling really means that very little assistance will be available. As well, this Bill does not address the question of the survival of small businesses, which is the most immediate concern of many small businesses today. Another concern is that this Bill applies to new equipment only. Many small businesses and farmers buy used equipment in an effort to keep cost to a minimum, and this Bill will not help in this regard. This Bill is also very vague and provides that far too much discretion be granted to the Government to make regulations concerning
April 11, 1983

operations of the program. The only things specified in the Bill are the 12 per cent ceiling, the 4 per cent maximum grant, the right of Government to get money back which was granted to those not entitled to the money, and the authority to make regulations.
Small businesses, as we all know, are generators of employment and income in every region and virtually every community in Canada. Small businesses provide important goods and services that might otherwise be unavailable or limited in type and quality. They are the mechanism for much of the innovation and the risk-taking that is essential to our economic system. They are also the source of new materials, concepts, production techniques and goods that larger enterprises would perhaps not be forced to develop. As well, the owners of small businesses are usually the backbone of the community in which they live, contributing to it in many ways at a personal level. In the case of Canada, the contribution made by the small business community is indeed impressive. The one million small businesses in Canada provide 42 per cent of the private sector employment in this country. They offer a rich diversity of projects and services and have been a major factor in industrial growth, innovation and job-creation.
While we are happy to see that interest rates have fallen somewhat in the past few months, we must be aware that the ceiling of 12 per cent spelled out in Bill C-136 will now mean that little or no assistance is provided to the small business people and farmers forced to resort to this type of borrowing. I suggest, therefore, that consideration be given to lowering the ceiling of 12 per cent, which would indeed be a step in the right direction. I would also suggest that this Government immediately work on de-regulating the business and farming communities in Canada and leave the business and farming communities which have the necessary expertise and experience to run their own businesses and enterprises. Let them do the job that they are both capable of doing. This is something which is totally lacking in Governments which have an abundance of theorists but totally lack practical and business-oriented people who know what it means to meet payrolls. This country was built on the sweat and toil of free entrepreneurs with little or no Government interference. Motivation, incentives, and the desire to better oneself were the key motivators toward the goal of success. Government intervention only serves to stifle those goals, and I believe the Government has interfered long enough. The results have been disastrous, to say the least. I believe it has had its turn and has been found wanting. I believe it is time for industry to remove the shackles of Government, assert their independence, and thus get our country back on track again to improve our economy, to reduce unemployment, and to eliminate and discourage inflation.
Small Business Investment Grants Act
