The House resumed consideration of Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 1 and 2 of Mr. Orlikow (p. 24327).

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am, I think, happy to speak on Bill C-136 but I am really not that overjoyed. While I agree with the thrust of what was originally contained in the budget of many moons ago, back in 1982, I want to say to the House most seriously that if there ever was an example of morass and stagnation in Government business, this simple little Bill, which is high in principle and very short in pages, is to me one of the best examples that we could find. I have no intention of involving the Minister who introduced the Bill in first reading on October 28 and second reading on November 8, 1982. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) is a very honourable man. I gather that this was his initial baby in the House since he obtained his new portfolio, and he was congratulated on the day the Bill was introduced.
Hear, hear!

I must say, Mr. Speaker, compared to a multitude of Bills that we have had in this House which actually give you a tendon problem in the elbow because they are so heavy and multi-faceted and contain many subjects, this Bill C-136 was quite unique. It has two and one-half pages and

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
six Clauses. It does all the things that other Members here today have said that it was intended to do, and it came at a time, of course, when interest rates were unconscionably exorbitant and in fact was to provide a base, a ceiling, of 12 per cent, giving a subsidy in effect, as I understand it from the very brief provisions of the Bill, of up to 4 per cent to reduce interest rates to 12 per cent. That is very commendable. No one objected to that. What I really cannot understand, as some Members have pointed out today, is why in the name of common sense are we debating this Bill today just one week and one day away from another budget. Today, other Hon. Members have asked what is going to happen in the budget of April 19 and whether small business, big business, individual taxpayers and the unemployed will get the help and assistance they so richly deserve from a Government that has been incompetent.
I do not know what is in the budget, and I do not think the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey) knows either. Small business and tourism are two areas which can do more to promote jobs and build the substructure for the country, which provides the sinews of the economy in taxes and jobs, than almost any other factor or feature of Government operations.
I am glad the dean of the House is with us today but I do not know whether he is going to be greatly excited about what I have to say. This matter was touched upon by the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) and I think it is something that is of increasing concern to Members of the House. Like Old Man River, this session just goes on and on. Today is the 487th day of sitting of the first session of this Parliament which started on April 14, 1980. Is it any wonder that the life has gone out of the Government and a lethargy has taken over that is suffocating any interest in regenerating the country? When a Government that is supposed to control its own business goes on and on like Old Man River with no focus, no direction and no definition, then things are serious.
I am not going to argue matters of procedure but today the Senate is supposed to give an answer to Senator Mcllraith who was a well respected House leader for the Government years ago. On Wednesday, March 30, he asked the Senate what the legal status was for the Parliament of Canada to consider anything, let alone another budget, when a couple of budgets had already been considered in this session but there had been only one Speech from the Throne. There have been budgets and financial statements and other statements of exculpation-they might even get up to five financial statements in this session as it drags on.
Bill C-136 is just two and a half pages and six clauses long. It was introduced for first reading on October 28, 1982 with only four speakers, taking a total of seven and a half pages in Hansard. The debate started at 7.25 p.m. and ended at 8.30 p.m. the same night. The Bill was then referred to Committee where it was debated in one session for an hour and a quarter
and was disposed of on November 23, 1982. Then, low and behold, it lost its priority. Interest rates started to change.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think the House is wasting time debating this Bill until we know what will be in the budget of April 19. That will do more to restore confidence than anything in the Bill. Although the Minister spoke in glowing terms about the $400 million provided in the Bill, I understand that he has reduced the amount to $60 million now. Perhaps he or someone else will be able to tell us the amount in the applications that have been approved or are still in front of the Minister at the present time. I venture to say that we are not dealing with $400 million or $60 million now.
I should like to know how necessary it is that we deal with this piece of legislation today. It has just been sitting there since it was dealt with in Committee on November 23. I surmise that the reason it has not been pushed ahead is that it has lost its relevance. Interest rates have come down. There may be a good psychological argument that because it was there, it helped bring interest rates down. I will give credit where credit is due, and if that factor, amongst others, helped bring interest rates down, I am pleased.
The report of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business shows that today 700,000 or 800,000 fewer Canadians are employed in small and medium-sized business than were employed in January 1981. The Bill would not have much effect on that situation anyway.
It is ironic, Mr. Speaker, that according to the terms of the Bill, it has already expired. As I understand the Minister's explanation, the Bill does not apply after March 31, 1983. The Bill was started with some fanfare, and it was not held up in the House. It has been kicking around since the budget of 1982 but was not pushed ahead. The Minister did not approach the House to get it through because there was a need for it. Interest rates went down.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, it is a great example of stagnation in the legislative program of the Government that we take the time of the House to deal with a Bill that is no longer relevant. I should like to know how many people are directly affected by it. If there are any, the Bill could have been passed by some type of House order and agreement with the Opposition. In principle, we are for the Bill, but the factors have changed so fundamentally that the whole thing is a farce.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a contribution to the debate on Bill C-136, not to cover old ground but merely to recognize that we are being asked to pass, almost retroactively, a measure that is quite unnecessary at this time and which will do nothing for small business in the months and years ahead. The costs and the burden of the various Government programs make it difficult for people to remain in business in Canada, and the Bill does not address those serious problems.
The Government has bungled its priorities once again. When this Party and the Party to my left from the end of 1979 until late last winter called for assistance with the high interest rates that affected home owners and small businesses, the
April 11, 1983

Government was preoccupied with finding ways to bail out its big corporate friends and totally ignored the plight of the small business sector.
With a lot of pushing from this side, the Government finally begrudgingly agreed to implement the Small Business Development Bond Program which was introduced by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in his budget of 1979. Had that program been adopted immediately, many of the small businesses which no longer exist in the country might have survived the worst economic depression since the mid-1930s.
We dragged the Liberals into the 1980s, screaming and kicking, and tried to get them to realize the plight of the small business sector. Today, in 1983, we are about to adopt legislation which is applicable only to March 31, 1983. It is designed to help people whose interest rates exceed 12 per cent, although the prevailing market rate is 12 or 12.5 per cent. The Bill is practically worthless.
The Government has failed to deal with the fundamental problems that have been crushing small businesses and leading to an unprecedented rate of bankruptcies. The small business sector employs more than 70 per cent of people who work in private agencies in the country. We have seen a massive and phenomenal rate of bankruptcies amongst those businesses which are the mainstay of our economy, and this has evolved from measures such as the National Energy Program which has destroyed the climate and the enthusiasm for investment in this country. It was compounded by the budget introduced by the former Minister of Finance on November 12, 1981, which was subsequently corrected and adjusted in December of that year, then replaced by another budget on June 28, 1982, then corrected by another economic statement in the autumn, and finally the residual measures were adopted in this House a few weeks ago by way of the amendments to the Income Tax Act, the Ways and Means legislation.
Then the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) introduced 26 new amendments to the Income Tax Act to enact measures which he did not want to accept as amendments to the principal Bill, Bill C-139, I believe it was, because he would have to admit that the Opposition had been right in much of their criticism of those various tax measures. But he introduced the changes retroactively after the Bill was passed, Mr. Speaker.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that all of this turmoil and confusion, this talk of taxing the imputed benefits of employees of small businesses, and the taxation of automobile allowances, the imposition of a regime of taxation on fuels, oil and gas and other energies which are used in the manufacturing and production of goods by our small business, all of these measures have imposed a punishing burden upon the small businesses of Canada.
Then there were the Statistics Canada experts who went around to many businesses with long and detailed forms which this Parliament never approved, with a myriad of complex and often very personal and penetrating questions, and these
Small Business Investment Grants Act
businessmen were told that they must comply under the threat of imprisonment or major fines. That, of course, takes away from the time they have to service their customers, to service their deficits and to make the financial and management decisions which are important to keep those businesses viable.
There is also the Metric Commission and the impact it has had on the retail sector, which consists of small businesses primarily, and the hassling of people who would sell gasoline by the gallon, carpeting by the yard and lumber by the 4 foot by 8 foot sheet size. We now have this very confused situation where you can still buy two by four lumber and four by eight sheets of plywood and three inch nails in building supplies, but you are not allowed to buy gasoline by the gallon if a merchant chooses to sell it that way, even though many Government agencies still dispense gasoline by the gallon and oil by the quart.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have this morass of costly and confusing burdens which this Government is imposing on the small business sector of this country. Then it asks us to come into Parliament and pass retroactively a piece of legislation which cannot have any benefit to the businesses of the country beyond this day. So we ask what the Government is doing about all of this other nonsense, the offshore purchasing policies, for example Mr. Speaker, where a number of semisubmersible lifeboats are to be purchased to supply the coastguard of Canada. Small business in my riding has produced such vessels satisfactorily, not only for the Canadian coastguard but for the coastguards of other nations and the major oil companies, the multinationals which are operating in the Arctic and off the East coast of Canada. These boats, which are produced in Richmond, British Columbia, are being used very successfully in those cases, but when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) decides to buy a new lifeboat, he goes offshore to purchase it because certain people within the search and rescue service have decided and predetermined that there is only one type of vessel which will meet their needs. It is not so bad to have a specific type of design in mind, but when you rule out the right of Canadian small businesses to bid competitively for the right to supply such systems, then there is something drastically wrong with Government policy in the purchasing areas. That, again, is another example of the tremendous imposition of costly burdens on the small business sector.
Certain provisions of the Official Languages Act are imposing costs indirectly upon small businesses which must compete with Government-run or Government-regulated agencies which do provide services in both official languages, even in some parts of the country where it is not necessary. Small businesses which are trying to provide competitive services are forced very often to print and to publish in both languages at a considerable additional cost to them even though there is no additional return at the sales counter.
We could well spend more time reviewing the banking practices within this country. I know that this Parliament, and the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, has

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
just gone through a major revision of the Bank Act, but, Mr. Speaker, if you had had occasion to visit your banker to borrow money, as I have had recently, you might be astounded at some of the extra costs which are being tacked on over and above the basic interest charge. For example, if you want a short-term loan for a couple of weeks, many of the Canadian chartered banks now charge you not only a set-up fee, and not only straight interest, but an additional service charge because you are not borrowing the money for long enough, which pushes the effective interest rate up to near usurious levels.
All of these measures and initiatives which have frustrated and hamstrung the small businesses of our nation have contributed to the present high levels of unemployment, which we learned about in the recent Statistics Canada figures which were debated earlier today in this House. To waste the time of the people of Canada in this Parliament in an attempt to enact legislation which is no longer effective, which is not going to be retroactive except with respect to certain applications which were entered into prior to March 31, 1983, just seems to be a ridiculous and foolish illustration of the total misdirection of priorities by this Liberal Government. As the Gallup poll indicated last week, I believe the people of Canada have had enough. They would like to throw this Government out and we would like to also.

Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-136, Small Business Investment Grants Act, be amended by adding immediately after line 21 at page 2 the following:
"5. (1) An order of the Governor in Council under section 4 shall be laid before Parliament not later than the fifteenth sitting day of Parliament after it is made.
(2)	A motion for the consideration of the House of Commons to the effect that an order referred to in subsection (1) be confirmed, signed by a Minister of the Crown, shall be filed with the Speaker of the House of Commons not later than the twentieth sitting day of Parliament after the said order has been laid before Parliament pursuant to subsection (1).
(3)	Where a motion for the consideration of the House of Commons is filed as provided in subsection (2), the House of Commons shall, not later than the sixth sitting day of Parliament following the filing of the motion, take up and consider the motion.
(4)	A motion taken up and considered in accordance with subsection (3) shall be debated without interruption for not more than three hours and, on the conclusion of such debate or at the expiration of the third such hour, the Speaker of the House of Commons shall forthwith, without further debate or amendment, put every question necessary for the disposition of the motion.
(5)	If a motion described in subsection (2) is taken up and considered by the House of Commons in accordance with subsection (3) but is not adopted by that House, the particular order to which the motion relates shall stand revoked.
(6)	If a motion described in subsection (2) is taken up and considered by the House of Commons in accordance with subsection (3) and is adopted by that House, the particular order to which the motion relates comes into force immediately on the adoption of the motion by the House of Commons."
and by renumbering the subsequent Clauses accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, far too often this House of Commons is presented with legislation such as is represented in Bill C-136, and it is with that in mind that Motion No. 3 was introduced.
Motion No. 3 requires that when an Order in Council is made, under the provisions of this Statute, the Order in Council must be put before Parliament and that there be a three-hour debate and a vote on that matter if it is required by Parliament. The concept here is to make sure that, when we have legislation which implies massive numbers of Orders in Council, somewhere along the line the people of Canada, by their elected representatives, should be able to say something about that type of legislation. This particular Bill in its definition, and the definition section is the kind of definition section that you are always concerned about, speaks about the word "prescribed". And what does "prescribed" mean? It means prescribed by regulation. Then when you get to the main granting section of the Bill, that is Section 3, it says, "On application to the Minister by a person who establishes .. . " what? In a form prescribed:
April 11, 1983

-that he is, pursuant to the regulations, eligible to receive a grant in respect of interest payable by the person on a prescribed small business investment debt- the Minister may, subject to the regulations, make a grant-
Well, the fact of the matter is that Section 4 of the Bill says:
The Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing anything that by this Act is to be prescribed and providing for all other matters and things as he deems necessary to carry out the provisions of this Act.
One begins to wonder what happened to legislation by Parliament if this type of uncontrolled regulatory power is allowed to exist. Yet it does, and it is a most dangerous type of precedent. Here we have a Bill which in no way controls the kinds of grants a Minister may make, other than that it cannot be for more than 4 per cent of the interest amount of the loan and cannot reduce the rate of interest on a loan to below 12 per cent. Other than that, there are no terms and conditions. The grants can be for anything. The grant could be to blueeyed Liberals. It could be to people engaged in raising marijuana. It could be to anyone engaged in any kind of business the Minister decided to prescribe. There is no control. The Minister could authorize a loan to what he describes as small business, which is not necessarily a small business under the Income Tax Act. It could be a small business like Canadair or de Havilland. They are small businesses. As a matter of fact, their profits are small. As a matter of fact, their profits are non-existent. Massey-Ferguson could qualify because they could be described as a small business under the regulation. If you think about it, as long as the subsidy is only 4 per cent and the interest rate is reduced to not less than 12 per cent, there is absolutely no limit to what could be granted under the terms of this Bill. It is open all the way.
It is with that in mind, Mr. Speaker, that we introduce this kind of amendment. I say to you, Sir, that it is absolutely essential that when legislation that must perforce give the Governor in Council power to make regulations is brought before the House, it must also curtail the power of the Governor in Council to bring forth those regulations. We have seen this problem in metric conversion where we have people raising before the courts of this country the issue of whether regulations made under the Weights and Measures Act are proper. We have that kind of section in this Bill where the Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing anything. When we pass legislation of that nature, what we have really done is say to our constituents that we are here for no purpose other than to give the Government power to do what ever the Government wants to do. In a very serious and real sense we have abandoned our responsibility to the people of Canada. We have left the door open for any kind of dictatorship the Party in power wants to impose upon the country. When we had before this House legislation concerning metrication, there was no suggestion at all that metrication would be compulsory. But it was compulsory because of the provision which allowed the Governor in Council to make regulations which were never contemplated by anyone in this House when the legislation was dealt with. The same possibility exists here.
The Minister says, quite properly, that he is not going to make any grants under this Bill unless they were applied for
Small Business Investment Grants Act
with respect to loans made prior to April 1. We will take him at his word and we may have a further matter to bring before this House later this afternoon in that regard. But as the Bill stands now, there is the possibility that a Minister of the Crown could come forward, maybe a year or two years from now, and decide to make grants to small-businessmen carrying on business in Corner Brook, Newfoundland, and only them. That would be quite proper under this Bill. There is no requirement that what was said in a budget debate in June, 1982 need apply. The Bill becomes a statute of Canada, and that allows the Minister to make regulations to allow any kind of a grant as long as it is not in excess of 4 per cent and it does not reduce the interest rate on a loan to below 12 per cent. So a Minister of the Crown-the current Minister, and he is a good Minister-may piously say that he would not do that type of thing, but this legislation does not tie the hands of any future Minister. No one else is bound by that. This Minister may not be the Minister responsible for small business a month or two down the pipe. Some other Minister may have a new jolly green program with new jolly green brochures for jolly green grants. He may want to, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) says, hand out some jolly green dollar bills to his jolly green friends. And, Sir, he can do it. All he has to do is to get the Governor in Council to pass the regulations, and away we go.
So I say to this House that when this type of provision is included in the statute, this House must insist on an amendment in the form that I have presented to this House this afternoon, a provision that these regulations may be tabled before Parliament and that there be a debate-not a long debate, but one of three hours-and it be brought to a vote so that Parliament has an opportunity to express itself with respect to regulations. It is on that basis, Sir, that this amendment is presented.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak to this amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). There is no question that the amendment is a good one in that it identifies once again one of the major weaknesses of Bill C-136. Section 3 of that Bill reads as follows:
On application to the Minister by a person who establishes in the form and manner prescribed that he is, pursuant to the regulations, eligible to receive a grant in respect of interest payable by the person on a prescribed small business investment debt obligation owed by him, the Minister may, subject to the regulations, make a grant to the person or his agent of such amount, not exceeding four per cent per annum of the principal balance outstanding from time to time of the debt obligation, as would reduce the effective rate of interest on the debt obligation for the period in respect of which the grant is made to not less than twelve per cent per annum.
In a nutshell, what that says is that the Minister may decide to target certain groups for particular incentive programs. It is possible that the Minister would identify under the terms and conditions in a set of regulations that this particular Bill ought

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
to apply to certain sectors of the small business community. Perhaps it would be small businesses involved with tourist services, perhaps those which are involved in the high-tech industry or those which are emphasizing the fishing industry or certain service industries.
What is important is that we must realize that it is open-ended. This amendment attempts to bring some accountability to the Government benches. If the Government wishes to target certain groups in the economy for some special assistance, then the purpose of this amendment is to have the Government come forward to Parliament and present the issue in such a way that Parliamentarians have an opportunity to react to this selective incentive program.
Quite frankly, I have little quarrel with that procedure. I like the idea of seeing the day when the Government of Canada will have an economic and industrial strategy in place which will enable it to target particular sectors of the economy for special encouragement and support. After all, this is not a particularly new concept. Many other countries spend a good portion of their budgets on the encouragement of certain industries. As a matter of fact, if we examine the Canadian Government's estimates carefully, we will find that this is already taking place today. There are complete sets of incentive programs for certain kinds of enterprises.
The problem concerns the fact that these programs lack any direction. They are not part of any particular strategic program and do not strive to obtain a particular goal. It is simply an ad hoc and random approach to whatever business is able perhaps to lobby most effectively or to whatever enterprise might bring a particular advantage to a selected region of Canada. These particular enterprises are being provided with certain incentives today. However, it is in the absence of a comprehensive industrial recovery program that these incentives are taking place. That is one of the major weaknesses of the program.
I am in favour of the concept of regulations being drafted that would provide encouragement for certain selected sectors of the economy which Canada sees as sectors that perhaps would bring some strategic advantage to the Canadian economy, which would provide us with a greater opportunity for world product mandating, or sectors of the economy that would give Canada a particular edge in world markets. Consequently, it is to those industries we should be giving some special attention.
As I indicated earlier, other countries do this and there is no reason why Canada should not do so as well. I am particularly concerned about this issue as a result of the information which has been provided to us lately with regard to the level of unemployment in Canada. We are presently facing a seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of 12.6 per cent. The Government of Canada tells us that this level of unemployment will be with us for some time in the future. It is saying that this is essentially a level of unemployment that Canadians must accept and consider to be a reality in the months ahead. I want to say that there are many of us who do not accept that and do not accept the premise that Canada is faced with a 12.6 per
cent seasonally adjusted unemployment level, a fact which must be accepted. I believe that we can see a slow economic recovery occur in our country with an economic strategy that recognizes that certain Canadian industries possess a strategic advantage which can be developed.
I suspect that the Minister whose Bill we are debating today, the Minister responsible for small businesses (Mr. Rompkey), has identified the tourist industry as one of the critical sectors where Canada has some advantage. The tourist industry is a sector which I believe ought to be receiving a great deal more attention than it is today. It is largely a sector of small enterprises and one which caters to the family business. It is a sector that is essentially Canadian owned and controlled and from which the profits of the enterprises remain in the country for further investment. It is the type of industry in which Canada obviously has a contribution to make in terms of world tourist markets. At the moment it does not receive particular encouragement from the Government of Canada nor, I suspect, from most of the provincial Governments.
If this particular Clause were part of Bill C-136, it would provide a mechanism for the Government of Canada to target tourism as an industry that it would like to encourage, support and nurture in a number of ways. For that reason I support what Clause 3 is attempting to accomplish in principle. However, the amendment of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, would provide an opportunity for Parliament to debate those special regulations and initiatives that the Government may be taking. For that reason, I hope the Minister responsible for small business gives some consideration to the amendment at present before the House.
There is no reason for being hesitant about the regulations. One becomes somewhat skeptical when Members opposite on the Government side say that they are not prepared to come to Parliament to disclose the new set of regulations as they change from time to time. While that may be expedient in terms of Government business, in terms of Parliament being able to provide its support to economic initiatives provided by the Government I suspect that there is no reason for this amendment being supported not only by Members of the Official Opposition and the NDP, but by Government Members as well.

Mr. Speaker, it would be nice if the Government Members opposite occasionally supported an amendment that made common sense. It has not been the practice of the House very often but perhaps this is one occasion when we can look for a few independent spirits on that side of the House to support us on an amendment which I suggest does make common sense.
I spoke earlier this day on the NDP amendment and mentioned the fact that an amendment would be moved later that dealt with something that is of considerable interest to me. In the course of my previous remarks, I ran out of time and forgot to draw to the Minister's attention how much more pleasant it would be to be standing in the House today dealing with a
April 11, 1983

piece of legislation which would be helping small business in a meaningful way and assisting small businessmen in this country. It is a tragedy to be standing here today when that type of legislation is not before us.
I hope that the Minister would know that the greatest problem facing Canadian small businesses today is that, first, far too many small-businessmen do not have equity financing and, second, they have trouble competing in the marketplace because the markets, to a large extent, have dried up. The small businessman is quite often at the mercy of the large multinational corporation which can ride out a period of economic difficulty much easier since it has a much wider asset base to draw upon.
If we were presently examining a piece of legislation which would provide equity rather than debt financing to small business, I am sure that Members on this side of the House- certainly those from the Progressive Conservative Party- would give such a sensible piece of legislation speedy passage, because it would be helpful to the small business sector. If we were standing here today to examine a piece of federal legislation which dealt with the purchasing policy of the federal Government, we would have to remember that it spends something in the order of $90 billion per year. The United States, our major competitor just to the south of us, has had in place for years and years a small business set-aside provision which encourages the development of small business by providing a protected share of market on federal Government purchasing for that small business sector. If we were to see a common sense piece of legislation which increased the market potential of the small business sector, it would obtain speedy passage from this side of the House. That is not the piece of legislation before us today. The one before us today is more than a year old in the sense of its promise and several months old in the sense of when it saw the light of day.
This is a Bill to provide up to 4 per cent relief to small businesses that have to borrow money. As soon as we deal with a Bill to provide some amount of interest relief to some segment of Canadian society, it forces us to consider the fact that it has been in a large measure the federal Government, its borrowing habits and its $30 billion deficit, that have caused interest rates to rise historically.
It is the federal Government or the Liberals opposite who over a period of years have competed in the marketplace to borrow money. They have competed against people who want to borrow money to mortgage their homes. Interest rates shot way up for people who wanted to obtain mortgages to purchase their first homes because the major competitor for those funds was the federal Government. With an unlimited chequebook, the federal Government went into the marketplace and bid with increasingly high interest rates to borrow funds. Thus every home owner in the country who had to mortgage his home was required to pay higher interest rates, or if he wanted to purchase a car or finance a small business. We have the villain, the Liberal Party of Canada represented by its Cabinet, driving up the costs of borrowing money over a period of years, and then bringing in a piece of legislation which says,
Small Business Investment Grants Act
"Are we not the good guys because we will give back some of that money?" This sounds attractive to many people, but when we look at the legislation, we must ask ourselves whether it tells us to whom the money will be given back or under what conditions it will be given back. The answer to these questions is no.
In this piece of legislation Members of Parliament really have no say on who is to benefit from this expenditure of tax dollars. We find in Clause 4 that the Order in Council shall decide. When we see those words, we know they really mean Cabinet, a select group of 30-odd Members opposite who meet in secret and decide what the regulations will be. It is through regulation that one gets control. I mentioned earlier today one regulation which the Cabinet opposite wants to include, that is, if small businesses in the country buy new pieces of machinery which meet the qualifications it decides, they will be given interest relief, but if they purchase used ones, they will not be given relief. In other words, if a small-businessman, who is cost conscious and has a business which is borderline and may go under, finds a bargain in terms of a used piece of equipment and borrows money to buy it, the federal Government is saying that he will pay the whole interest charge. Let us say that the piece of equipment can be purchased for $10,000. Then he pays the whole interest shot. But the Government is saying that if he goes out and purchases a new piece of equipment, perhaps no better but simply because it is new, and he pays $20,000 for it, then the Government will give him some help. In other words, if he drives up the cost of doing business, the Government will help. It will help feed inflation and help inflation to grow, but if he is cost conscious, it will not help. If he tries to keep costs down, and therefore the cost to consumers, and tries to help a small business compete against multinational organizations, the Government will not help. But if he is wasteful and buys more than he needs, the Government will help. It is like a carrot to increase inflation and ultimately the bankruptcy rate of small business.
This is not something which Parliamentarians in their wisdom decided to do. This is something which Cabinet decided to do, an appointed body, appointed by one man, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which meets in secret and issues regulations. The powers are enormous. This type of clause in such a piece of legislation is at its most basic level anti-democratic. The voters of the country vote for the people they want to come to this Chamber to represent their views and perspective. Then what are we given a chance to do? We are simply given a chance to vote to give Cabinet more powers, to give that appointed body more powers.
I come from Calgary. The unemployment rate, the vacancy rate and all such indicators of economic difficulty, have risen enormously in the last year or year and a half. They have had the highest rate of increase in the country. Why is that? It is because the federal Cabinet took unto itself the power to regulate far too many industries, but in particular the oil and gas industry. It was done with such understanding that half the jobs and half the economic spin-offs around the country were

April 11, 1983
Small Business Investment Grants Act
killed. Today we have a Minister of Energy who will roll back prices when they are already less than 75 per cent of the world price. That takes money out of the hands of businesses. It forces them into the marketplace to borrow. Then we will have a piece of legislation like this one. As the interest rates rise, the Government will help, but it will not produce any more oil or any more jobs. The situation comes about because it is not Parliament which decides, in all its collective wisdom. It is a small group called Cabinet which takes too much power unto itself. Approximately 3,500 Cabinet-type regulations a year mean that none of them are looked at with the kind of care and attention they deserve.
I hope Hon. Members opposite will rise later in the House on this amendment, take that power away from Cabinet and put it back in Parliament where it belongs so that fewer mistakes will be made in the future.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say that I support this amendment very strongly because it really brings back into the House the responsibility which belongs here, rather than allowing it to float through an Order in Council without any reference back to the House.
There are too many things which the Government has done without our knowledge. There is a great deal that we cannot know about because it is a diverse economy and we cannot know everything about everything at all times. It is very important that legislation concerning small business be referred back to the House. I believe an over-all overhaul should be implemented immediately. Once that comes in and there is self-monitoring and perhaps private funding for a portion of it, we will not need to bring it back to the House.
The only reason legislation has to come back to the House is because of the spending of taxpayers' money. I do not think we should spend taxpayers' money. Instead we should encourage industry to survive on its own. That is really the thrust of my remarks.
I think this is a stopgap Bill. I am sure the Liberals will come up with a total, encompassing small business policy. I really believe they will do it some day. It may not be in time because we may be the Government and we will have the opportunity to put it in. Believe me, we will put in broad small business policy.
Talking about the problems in Canada, an interesting paper was put out by the University of Western Ontario giving an analysis of Canadian banking and the problems with the branch bank system, the lack of trained people to help the individual, help the corporation, assess what is required and possibly to implement.
In the United States there are many small banks, although fewer than there used to be. They are getting more into central banking because of the demand for dollars. The small bank in each town, the owner, who happened to be the banker, knew what was going on. He knew the business. He would get monthly statements and regular quarterly statements. He knew exactly where they were at. He would find people who in
a true pioneer spirit, would invest capital into a company so that he could provide additional borrowing.
That is one of the areas where we in Canada have failed. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) brought out that we should have an edge in world trade. I agree with him totally. There are a great many things on which he and I agree.
What happens to us in this country is that we have to borrow so much money and pay interest on that money to try to get a business going. We do not have enough equity money coming into the market and risk capital that may make a bit more money in the future. As Members know, at the beginning it is hard to make money. It takes seven years for an industry to get under way. That is what is really addressed in this piece of literature from the University of Western Ontario.
Relating to this, I am fairly aware of what happens in Japan and the reason for their success. A great deal of it relates to the "assist export trade". In many ways the Government gets involved. In the pure financing of businesses in Japan, there are ten separate organizations. They have city banks, local banks, long term credit banks and trust banks. There are ten that split this up. It is not a monopoly they are dealing with.
An independent small entrepreneur in Japan has a variety of sources from which to get money. In addition, many of the small businesses in Japan, unfortunately, are dependent upon some of the majors. Some of the majors assist them at times when growth is not that great or when they are over-supplied. They assist them in financing their inventory. Some do, some do not, but it makes a tremendous difference.
These Japanese banks not only lend money on debt but on equity. There is a variety. I am looking at a comparison. In Canada we have four sources, of which 74 per cent are the chartered banks. The balance is split between mortgage loan companies, trust companies and local credit unions.
Germany has a much broader spectrum, as do most of the European countries, because they have merchant banks that really go into venture capital. Then they carry on. They put so much in through equity, and the balance through debt. We do not have the same facility for small business in this country. We have lost the entrepreneurial spirit. It is very difficult to get a business going. It is very difficult to raise equity capital, no matter how good the idea.
I know there is an exception. The Minister knows about it. The exception now is high technology firms. That has sex appeal. It has the possibility of a balloon, of really growing rapidly. Strangely enough, Canadians believe it has the possibility of failing. That is free enterprise, the right to succeed and the right to fail. That is why we should not step in and try to prop up marginal operations.
We have to provide something to give them a base to work from. With the tremendous rise and fall of interest rates, industry and business cannot operate. They cannot live with it. They cannot budget for it. When we have those high interest rates, we have a reduction in sales. You get a double-whammy.
April 11, 1983

While I am on sales, I will put in another dig. They hit the salesman twice as hard in the year that sales go down by charging him twice as much for standby charges on his car. That was unfair during 1982, one of the worst periods we have gone through.
In Canada we do not have incentives to get people to invest in small business. There are no incentives. One of our plans was to remove capital gains on private business. Perhaps that would attract more money. I would rather see Canadian pension funds putting some funds into small business rather than buy more preferred shares in Massey-Ferguson. I have nothing against Massey-Ferguson. I think it is great to keep that organization going, but it may be an industry of the past. Hopefully, something can be resolved for them, but we should provide a proper financing vehicle outside of Government. That is where we are failing. The individual really does not need the Government to be involved if we have a proper financial system or if we had a mini stock market to cover small businesses trying to go public.
Part of the trouble with that is that brokers take such a large piece of a small deal. Perhaps there is a way around it through the banks. I do not know. We have to address this whole problem.
In our amendment we say that we want to vet this in front of the House. Then we could make some suggestions. We could all think about creating jobs and bringing something forward. That is what it is all about. We are talking about the people of this country, Canadians. I am talking about Canadian business.
The Liberal Government is nationalistically inclined. I agree that Canadian ownership is good. Young people should be given an opportunity to own their own business. We should do whatever we can for them. Again, this Bill is a stopgap, a bandaid. It will not solve the critical problem because business cannot operate on 12 per cent interest rates. That is too high.
Not so many years ago if a man in industry could get a 15 per cent return on his investment, he was doing extremely well. Then it went up to 20 per cent. At 12 per cent it is very marginal, a potential of at least 3 per cent.
Let us look where we are going. We will not come out of the recession quickly. It will take a long time. Thank heavens it will be gradual. Possibly this time we will come out with a better economic base than we had in the past. I hope it is not a sharp turn-up. I hope the Government does not come out with gimmicks to push it straight up and then it will come straight down. If we go up too quickly, and we have seen this happen, interest rates go up. To prove my point, if interest rates go to 20 per cent, this Bill will be of little help to the man paying 20 per cent interest. If he gets only 4 per cent off that, he still has 16 per cent, and that is far more than any small business can afford.
1 speak very highly of the amendment. I support it. I wish the Government would consider it. Members of Parliament deal with small business people in their constituencies. We
Small Business Investment Grants Act
want to give them answers. We want to know the problems. We do not know them when everything is done by Order in Council. I ask the Government to accept this amendment. Please allow us to review what is happening so that there are not so many regulations, so many powers, and so many changes to be made by the Government without its having to come to the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, just briefly to speak to it, I believe that it is good that we have finally come to a conclusion on this particular portion of the Bill. The original concept of the Bill was that grants would be made to reduce interest rates by up to 4 per cent and reduce them to 12 per cent for business.
As has been pointed out in the debate so far today, interest rates have very much ameliorated since the budget of June 28, 1982. There have, however, been a number of people who have made application thinking the Bill would go through in accordance with the brochures issued by the Government. The concept of this amendment is to allow those people to continue to receive the benefit of the grant. The Government at no time suggested to people that they could continue to take advantage of this Bill after March 31, so nobody has been harmed. It is our view that it is imperative, though, that the Bill not have any validity after the end of March or the first of April, as you pointed out, Sir, simply because to do so would leave an open-ended piece of legislation that could be used by some subsequent Minister or some subsequent Government to enter into a rather extensive loan or grant program, and it is on that basis that we are happy with this amendment.
We feel the amendment solves the problem. It looks after those who have been involved and made application under the Bill. It allows the Bill to be completed and wound up, but it leaves this whole possibility of further grants under this legislation not available. It also solves the problem of the amendment that I spoke on earlier that was negatived on division, the amendment with respect to reviewing Orders in Council that provide for grants and the like. Since the effect of the Bill will now be terminated as of April 1, 1983, by virtue of
the amendment I hope this Parliament will accept it. Should we pass it, then I suspect we will have solved the problem. On that basis, Mr. Speaker, I think we should perhaps move to the next stage of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: that the Bill be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on third reading of the Bill. I appreciate that the amendment offered by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) was accepted by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Rompkey). It will add a little common sense to the Bill. It would have been ridiculous to spend a day passing a Bill with its application limited to March 31. The amendment at least makes it a sensible Bill.
There is one thing that I would like to say in connection with the Bill and legislation in general. The Bill is a typical example of procedures that ought not to be followed. It was introduced on October 28 for first reading. On November 8 it was presented for second reading and four Members spoke. It then went to Committee, and today it is before us for debate at report stage and third reading. Between November 8 and today, April 11, businesses were going bankrupt and into receivership. Some closed their doors, yet we took five months to bring the Bill back to the House. Something has to be done about this procedure, Mr. Speaker, because it does not make sense.
A few weeks ago the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) and I had the pleasure of attending a seminar in England which was also attended by people from 18 Commonwealth countries. No one there could understand why we started a session in 1980 and are still involved in it. A number of them said this would not be tolerated in their country.
This is supposed to be a smart manoeuvre, but not as far as the people of Canada are concerned, Mr. Speaker. There should have been at least three sessions of this Parliament, but we are still involved in the first. There should have been three Throne Speeches, but there has only been one. Does that mean that the Government has no programs to offer for the future? Was everything included in the first Throne Speech in 1980? The country needs new material and new programs, Mr. Speaker. It has been denied the right to a Speech from the Throne for two years.
To some degree this Parliament is modelled after the Mother of Parliaments although in the last few years we have ignored many of its traditions. In September or October every year the Queen goes to Westminster to read the Speech from the Throne. The only exception to this is when an election falls in the middle of the term. Otherwise there is a session every year, a Speech from the Throne every year, a budget every year and Private Members' time every year. That has been denied to the people of Canada.
We should not tolerate this type of thing, Mr. Speaker. It ignores the basis of Parliament where people have the right to speak and debate programs. Under our parliamentary system, Members have the right to raise any subject at all during the
Adjournment Debate
debate on the Speech from the Throne. We have been denied that since 1980.
We have had three budgets. The country would be in a much better shape if we had done without two of them- especially the budget of November 12, 1981. It ruined a great number of our industries. It sent the petroleum, oil and gas industries right down the tube, and hundreds of people became unemployed as a result. It touched almost every sector of industry. The next budget tried to correct some of the wrongs of the first but it only added to our difficulties.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had called a new session in 1982 and in 1983, budgets would have been introduced as a matter of course and would have received attention. Instead, the Government has brought in mini budgets which were largely prepared by bureaucrats who wanted to get something through the House. The Minister did not even have a chance to go through them, otherwise they would never have introduced some of the nonsense that was in them.
Some of the items in the Bill prevent farmers and businessmen from retiring today. People who spent 40 or 50 years for their lives building a nest egg so that they could retire in dignity find that they cannot. The Government did away with annuities. In the first budget it said that people would have to pay a capital gains tax and that even though they received instalment payments, they would have to pay on the whole thing. This made it impossible for a farmer to sell his land to his son or daughter or his hired man or anybody else. It just about stopped the movement of land in all parts of Canada.
That was part of a budget that was brought in without thought for the people who pioneered this country. That could not happen in the Mother of Parliaments because a budget comes down regularly there. Her Majesty The Queen would have been available to read the Speech from the Throne in the fall of each year and it would have outlined the programs so that people would know what was going on.
The whole situation has been confused by the actions of the Government in carrying one session on month after month after month. This Bill is an example. Were it not for the attitude of the Minister, it would have been almost worthless. It would have expired before it was passed. It was limited to March 31 and today, on April 11, we are debating third reading.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REPORT ON MEETING IN PORTUGAL-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MAKE STATEMENT
NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REPORT ON MEETING IN PORTUGAL-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MAKE STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the adjournment debate in relation to a question I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 23, two or three weeks ago, concerning a meeting that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) was attending in Portugal, at which time, according to the United States press, Caspar Weinberger, was "to consult the allies on controversial NATO plans to deploy United States Pershing II and Cruise missiles in December". My question which appears at page 24067 of Hansard reads as follows:
Can the Prime Minister assure the House that, on his return, the Minister of National Defence will make a statement on motions to inform the House and the country what Canada's current position is on this very important subject?
The Minister went on from Portugal to China, and circumnavigated the world during the Easter holidays. He is now back and the Canadian people are to be no wiser for the trip.
In a second answer that very day the Prime Minister, in response to my supplementary question, said, as reported at page 24067 of Hansard:
I repeated it this morning to Vice President Bush, that there has been no Cabinet decision to test the Cruise.
By that, of course, he meant the Cruise missile.
This is the position in which the House finds itself; that we have conflicting statements from two Members of Cabinet, in this case one from the Prime Minister and one from the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan). The conflicting statement by the Minister of Justice when he was Secretary of State for External Affairs was given in a disarmament debate which is recorded at page 16741 of Hansard of April 29, 1982, as follows:
Following the decision of 1979, President Carter requested some 18 months ago that we allow one of the proposed missile systems, the Cruise Missile system, to be tested in Canada. It is the Carter request, which was subsequently adopted by the Reagan administration, which has been accepted by the Canadian cabinet.
The Prime Minister, of course, has said there has been no Cabinet decision to test the Cruise. I would like to point out that this quotation from the then Secretary of State for External Affairs was not given in the "hurley-burley" of Question Period. This statement was made during an Opposition Day. The Minister would have had at least 24 hours' notice of the subject matter of that debate. His Department would have prepared a speech for him, in all probability, and it would have been gone over carefully by several other people to make sure there were no errors or omissions. There is no excuse for a Minister to say something that is not true and factual in the middle of a prepared speech.
On March 24, 1982, over a year ago, the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence records that the Minister of Justice said, referring to two questions, and I quote:
The first one really is dealing with the testing of the Cruise missile system. This was a proposal that was put forward to Canada not by the Reagan
administration but by the Carter administration, some 18 months ago. As I indicated, it was considered by cabinet during 1981 and we agreed to proceed with it at that time, to proceed to try to negotiate an agreement with the United States, a framework agreement, which would cover not only this kind of testing but other kinds of testing as well.
He is saying that the proposal which was agreed to by the Cabinet was the one on testing of the Cruise missile.
Again before the same Standing Committee of External Affairs and National Defence on May 4, 1982, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
We have made a decision in principle in favour of the testing of the Cruise missile. That is, we have accepted it in principle. We have not accepted it in the context of a particular subagreement, nor have we even finished the negotiation of the overall agreement.
So it affects Cruise missile testing; no doubt about it.
Then on July 23, 1982, in the House of Commons, in reply to a question by the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), the then Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
Madam Speaker, a decision on principle on this matter was reached by the Canadian Government last year, that we would enter into negotiations with the United States with a view to having such testing, and also with a view to having a large agreement-In fact, not only have we not proceeded with that, but negotiations have not been completed on the over-all umbrella agreement.
On February 14, to bring it much closer to the present, we find the Prime Minister starting to back away. In answer to a question in the House of Commons as reported at page 22804 of Hansard, he said:
-whether the reference to tht by the former Secretary of State for External Affairs was not based upon an inaccurate memory of what President Carter had requested ... I cannot say ...
So he is intimating that the current Minister of Justice has an inaccurate memory and does not know what has happened.
On February 15, the following day, he had this to say in answer to another question:
It is not a matter of getting out of the agreement to test the Cruise. There has been no agreement to test the Cruise.
That is exactly the opposite of what his Minister was saying.
On March 15, 1983, in answer to a question in committee by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) as to whether there has been a request by the U.S. to permit them to test the Cruise missile guidance system in Canada, the current Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) said:
No. There has been no request.
That is a flat contradiction of his predecessor.
We have been led up the garden path by three different Cabinet Ministers going in three different directions. Would the Government please tell us what its position is on this vital matter and quit making fools of its members in the process?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REPORT ON MEETING IN PORTUGAL-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER MAKE STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, the Minister returned from his trip only this morning,
April 11, 1983

and it was his intention to report to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on April 19, on matters relating to the nuclear planning group meeting in Portugal. At this time I cannot answer all the questions of the Hon. Member, but I can make the following statement:
The Minister attended the semi-annual meeting of NATO's nuclear planning group just prior to proceeding to the midEast, Asia and Australia. At that meeting the defence Ministers reaffirmed the position taken by heads of state and Governments in June, 1982, that deterrence and defence, together with arms control and disarmament, are integral to the main purpose of the alliance. That is, to prevent war, safeguard democracy and to build the foundations of a lasting peace.
As expected, the deployment by NATO of intermediate range nuclear missiles dominated the proceedings. It was widely agreed that the Soviet Union had only been brought to the negotiating table at all as a consequence of the two-track December, 1979 decision. A strong consensus emerged that the governments of the alliance should continue to support implementation of both tracks of that decision. It was also agreed that, although the zero option should be maintained as a desirable goal, the time was right for taking an initiative in Geneva on an interim agreement on ceilings which would not in itself prevent deployment of NATO systems later this year. NATO ministers considered that the Soviet Union had not made any proposals which recognized the legitimate security interests in the West, and that the Andropov proposal, based upon compensation for British and French strategic forces, was completely unacceptable.
Apart from the intermediate force discussions, the Minister's attention was drawn to the continued build-up of Soviet strategic nuclear forces, including sea and air-launched Cruise missiles. The United States provided a brief account of the status of strategic arms reduction talks.
During the discussion the United States Secretary of Defence and NATO Secretary General Luns acknowledged the visible contribution made by Canada to NATO solidarity in approving the umbrella agreement under which Cruise missile flight testing could be authorized.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-INVESTMENT IN CORPORATE SECTOR-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PROMOTE INVESTMENT
THE ECONOMY-INVESTMENT IN CORPORATE SECTOR-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PROMOTE INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 22, 1983, I asked two questions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Those questions involved the necessity
Adjournment Debate
to provide greater incentives in this country for equity investment in order to get the country rolling again.
It is abundantly clear from the debate today that most Members who went back to their ridings discovered that both large and small businesses are desperately short of real capital. This does not surprise me since our tax laws as they exist today make it more advantageous for a person to lend money than to subscribe money to a company in capital.
Equity investment is hard to come by, by virtue of the fact that our tax system, in almost every instance, treats those who lend money more favourably than those who put their money at risk by buying shares in a company or by the common stock approach. Consequently, businesses all across the country do not have the freedom to move.
During the past few years, the last two or three in particular, we have seen an entire series of bankruptcies, insolvencies and receiverships which have largely been caused by the fact that businesses have been borrowing money. That borrowed money has had to bear interest. The reason businesses have had to borrow money is that they have not been able to encourage people to invest money as a solid capital investment.
When one examines the tax system, one finds, as the Lortie Commission found, that when corporate tax and personal tax applicable to dividends on equity investment are combined, the total tax paid on that money, that is at risk and earning in a company, is greater than the taxes applicable if a person simply loaned the money to the company in the first place. That being the case, there is really no incentive in the system to encourage people to invest and put their money at risk.
One suggestion made in the Lortie Commission Report was to somehow index capital investment so that indexed capital investment would be treated on the basis that if and when a capital investment is withdrawn from a company it would have the same purchasing power as when it was put in. The reason for that proposal is, of course, that most capital gains, or alleged capital gains, in this country are not that at all, but really a reduction in the purchasing power of the dollar.
Let me give an example. If one invested $1,000 in 1973 and was able to sell that investment in 1983 for what one would think would be 100 per cent profit, $2,000, that $1,000 would not have in fact been made. In fact, expressed in 1973 terms, that individual would have lost $228. Under our tax system one would be taxed on the basis of having made a $1,000 gain when in truth one lost $228. This kind of thing goes on day after day in our marketplace, so that people who have any sense at all refuse to put their money at risk unless the hope and dream is that that money at risk will do far better than 100 per cent in ten years. In fact, one would have to make something in the neighbourhood of 150 per cent over a ten-year period. This is not always practical. Indeed, one begins to wonder whether such investors have been tasking the hemlock of optimism far beyond what is realistic.
In the new budget to be presented by the Government on April 19, it is essential that it do something with respect to

April 11, 1983
Adjournment Debate
capital gains tax. In my view capital gains tax is anti-productive, discriminatory and unfair. We would be far better off as a country if we abolished it. We have to put into the investment community some sizzle, some hope, some drive. That sizzle, hope or drive is the possibility of making a profit. When one puts money at risk, one is behind the debt instruments-the debt has to be paid, the interest to the banks has to be paid. Whether or not that debt money in the company is really earning profits for the company, it has to be paid. The investor in a company only receives what is left after expenses, the bottom line. Profits and losses are not far apart because we are talking about the bottom line. Surely in a growing country we must make it possible in our budgets for those who invest to have an opportunity to make a profit and be well rewarded, or far better rewarded than those who just lend money.
Our present tax system militates in favour of the lenders of money, banks, trust companies and guaranteed investment certificate holders, but does not do anything for the risk taker, the person we really need to go out and create the jobs we so badly demand. As of today, 12.6 per cent of the population has been statistically determined to be unemployed. In truth there are well over two million Canadians either unemployed or so under-employed as to not really be treated as employed. They want to work and should be working. We must change the system to encourage growth, production, new investment and new opportunity.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-INVESTMENT IN CORPORATE SECTOR-REQUEST FOR MEASURES TO PROMOTE INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue raised by the Hon. Member is one on which there has been very valuable consultation with the public, based upon discussion papers presented by the Government. In June of last year, the discussion paper entitled, "Inflation and the Taxation of Personal Investment Income" was released. The Lortie consultative committee, to which the Hon. Member referred, reported to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), supporting the concept of a registered shareholder investment plan. The Minister of Finance has indicated agreement in principle with such a plan but, as the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) knows, its details are a budgetary matter, as are measures that might be taken to support new equity investment in the corporate sector.
The broader issue, the adjustment of business taxation for inflation, was addressed by both the discussion paper to which I referred and the Lortie committee. The Committee suggested a study of comprehensive inflation accounting, recognizing the major issues which would arise in any such inflation accounting system. The discussion paper referred to the complexity of such a system, possible redistributions of tax liabilities among sectors, and international complications as important unanswered questions.
Accounting groups in Canada and elsewhere have been debating these points for several years, and as evidence of their complexity there is no consensus on the best approach. In Canada, larger companies are beginning to provide inflation adjustment on an essentially experimental basis, but the methods are not sufficiently developed to serve as a basis for a
tax system. Whether it is desirable to undertake such a major modification of the tax system deserves serious reflection, and is to be determined by the Minister of Finance.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South appears most concerned about equity investment opportunities. Interest rates have fallen, as has inflation. Equity markets have been performing well and the basis has thus been laid for new equity issues. The Government is very aware of the importance of a sound equity basis for Canadian business, and the need for building on the recovery which is evident in equity markets. The budget speech is the appropriate place to learn of any new initiatives. The Hon. Member will naturally have to wait for the speech to know about any specific actions intended.
Finally, I would note that the Lortie committee addressed one approach suggested by the Hon. Member, elimination of capital gains tax. The committee indicated that it seriously considered the desirability of this course of action, but concluded it would not be desirable.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REPORTED PURCHASE OF CAST CORPORATION
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REPORTED PURCHASE OF CAST CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 25 I raised a question with respect to the CNR purchase of Cast and the contemplated purchase of Sofati, container operators, both centred in the city of Montreal, and the impact of the decision of the Crown corporation to act in this fashion.
I also raised the issue of whether the CTC had in fact held its public hearings-it has not-in respect to the Crown corporation's purchase. The Minister said that CTC had considered the matter. It became very obvious that if it had, it was in private, behind closed doors or in camera. The decisions are not publicly known. It was for that reason I initially asked the question.
The Minister said it was not a philosophical decision, not a socialist type of decision. I somewhat disagree with that. I feel that the tendency of this Government is further presented to the public by the inclination of the Crown corporation, CNR, to get further involved in shipping structures as they relate to Canada and its international trade. I am not at all sure that that necessarily puts it under the best management or that that is the best place for CNR to spend its money.
It goes further than that. It indicates that CNR is a free wheeling organization which does not have to comply with regulations that would be imposed on the private enterprise structure. It is in fact a free wheeling, go-ahead deal, similar to many other Crown corporations to which we have extended the use of the public purse without any necessity of getting approval for the use to which they put the money.
I want to point out to the House and the Minister that if we continue to centralize, CNR, Cast and the general shipping of Canada by water to the international world in the city of Montreal, this will have a serious detriment on the rail services
April 11, 1983

for freight into Atlantic Canada. The further this service declines, the more expensive it will become. The more expensive it becomes, the less attractive it will be to customers, national or international. When we moved Cast out of Halifax, we reduced the volume of traffic on the CNR. With that reduced volume, the unit cost has to go up.
The general policy of the Government had been that in the port system of Canada there should be a user pay situation. Is this going to apply in Montreal? If, for instance, a shipment came into Montreal in winter, or to any of the St. Lawrence; the Strait of Northumberland, Gulf of St. Lawrence ports, then ice breaking service is available to those ports at no cost. This puts the year-round ports, particularly that of the city of Saint John, in a position of very serious disadvantage. If there are free ice breaking services for the St. Lawrence area, it certainly will be detrimental to the user pay system which is imposed on the port of Saint John. This should be addressed. Ice breaking should either become a user pay service or compensatory steps should be taken to restore the port of Saint John to its historic position.
I also draw attention to the fact that National Harbours Board ports, including the Saint John port, are on a user pay basis. That is not the case with the commission ports or the other ports not under the National Harbours Board. Is it to be the continuing policy of the Government of Canada to make investments in the ports in the St. Lawrence and the north shore of New Brunswick which will be competitive with installations already bought by the Government of Canada in the port of Saint John? This is something of very serious concern.
I earlier cited in this House that the Port of Rimouski was built up and improved for the handling of wood products from Canada. That was after the four-term structure in the City of Saint John had been built with provincial help, and it went directly into competition with that terminal. That terminal is one of the most efficient in the world; its efficiency cannot be duplicated in other ports.
Are we then going to have Government pressure to expand other ports in the St. Lawrence Valley, in the north east of New Brunswick, to come into competition with already paid-for Government construction? Are we going to get DREE or other grants which will not be capitalized? Are we in fact going to capitalize them and impose upon them the philosophy of user pay?
Adjournment Debate
I must say that I think the transportation structure in general has mitigated against the best interests of the Port of Saint John, and against Atlantic Canada, both in relation to freight rates and to the preferences which have been extended to the Commission Port in conflict and in competition with the user-pay National Harbours Port.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REPORTED PURCHASE OF CAST CORPORATION

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is dead wrong when he says that the CN Crown corporation is not subject to the regulations to which the private sector companies are subject. The whole philosophy behind Crown corporations is that they must compete with private member companies, and they are treated as private companies and must compete on that basis. He was wrong when he said that Crown corporations are treated differently by the Government.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) clearly indicated to the Hon. Member in his answer of March 25 that whatever decision is arrived at with respect to CN and Cast, it will be subject to Government and CTC approval. Discussions have indeed taken place between these companies but no approval has been granted to a specific proposal by CN.
Faced with such a proposal, the Government would have to weigh several considerations. One is the competitive position of CN. As the Hon. Member knows, CP recently entered into an arrangement with Dart and Manchester Lines to provide an integrated Trans-Atlantic container service. Containers represent a healthy source of revenue for CN, and the company is obviously looking for ways of preserving this traffic.
Another aspect the Minister would have to look at is that of multi-modalism. There is a trend in transportation today toward door-to-door service: goods may move with one carrier, a development that is efficient and to the client's advantage. Cast was a pioneer in this area and CN, even with its minority interest, was able to benefit and better serve its customers.
The Government would also, of course, take into account the impact of any proposal by CN on ports in Atlantic Canada, such as Saint John and Halifax.
